He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise today with pleasure to lead off debate on Bill C-363. It is a very simple bill as members of the House will know by looking at it.
It is a one paragraph bill and I will read it for the record. It states that subsection 120(8) of the Excise Tax Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor under limitation section 8: "No rebate shall be paid under this section unless the application therefor is filed with the minister before 1993".
What does that mean? It is very simple. When the Government of Canada set out to change the old manufacturers' sales tax, the old federal sales tax, the replacement tax was called the goods and services tax. I know that all members of the House are aware of the new tax.
Part of the implementation of the the GST was a rebate mechanism so that businesses across Canada could look at their inventories and determine how much federal sales tax was in their inventory. In the old system of federal sales tax or manufacturers' sales tax, when a retailer bought merchandise from a manufacturer, built into the purchase price was the existing federal sales tax. The government established a rebate system. There
were a few other numbers, but primarily 8.1 per cent of a retailer's inventory would be eligible for a rebate.
When the tax was implemented on January 1, 1991 the rebate was available to companies for their year-end inventory but they had to file within one year of year end. Basically they had to file in 1991 for their end of
1990	inventory. Businesses generally filed throughout 1991.
However, at the end of 1991, people checked their returns from previous years and discovered that some people had not filed for a number of reasons. Perhaps it was a very small business and its accounting systems were not up to the standards of large corporations. Or, if it was a partnership, one thought the other had filed the return when it was not done. Maybe it was found in a subsequent audit.
I should point out that in my constituency I had three businesses come to me concerning this situation. One was a very small business which was eligible for about $8,000 in rebate. They found, having done their own returns the previous year, business had grown a little bit. In 1992 they hired an accountant. The accountant looked back at their 1991 returns and mentioned to them that they had missed out on their inventory rebate because it had not been filed.
This company had an inventory just under $100,000 and its sales were in the range of $300,000 a year. It had missed out on its $8,000 inventory rebate because its owners did not have the expertise to file in the first year. The accountant filed on their behalf but they were not eligible for the rebate.
Another company had a larger inventory. Again it was not a huge company but was eligible for an $80,000 rebate. Its owners thought they had filed in May 1991 but it was nowhere to be seen. They inquired in October
1991	concerning their rebate. They thought they had filed for it in May 1991. There was no record of the rebate, possibly through some sloppiness within the company. In January 1992 they sent in their rebate application and missed the deadline by 12 days. This is another company that was unable to get a refund of that inventory rebate.

Private Members' Business
Who does this legislation affect? It certainly does not affect General Motors of Canada, the large manufacturing companies or the large retailers. They all have the accounting systems, the professionalism, to make sure their rebate applications were sent in on time.
This helps small business, those people who simply because of size did not have the resources to file their applications at the right time, or in some cases through sloppiness did not file, or they were too busy trying to deal with the recession, employ people and sell the goods they had to go back and file later.
The reason I am bringing this bill forward is to make it possible for an extension for all those who did file in 1992, only to be told they had filed too late. We have the records of who all those people are, I am sure, within the Department of National Revenue. This would provide an opportunity for all those small businesses to get an infusion of money they were eligible to have given back to them in the form of a rebate, to receive it back into their businesses as cash flow.
The government prides itself on its activities with small business. In fact the Minister of National Revenue, in releasing a document on March 18, 1992, talked about a tax fairness package. I would like to quote from a press release that was issued in relation to that tax fairness package.
Speaking at the Macdonald Cartier Club, Mr. Jelinek noted that "the Fairness Package demonstrates my commitment to a simpler and fairer tax system. It will allow for common sense in dealing with taxpayers who, because of personal misfortune or circumstances beyond their control, are unable to meet deadlines or comply with rules."
"We must now concentrate on making the system more open-We cannot expect Canadians to have to dig through our policies and directives to discover what their rights are. It is up to us to take the initiative to reach out and make sure people know and understand how to take advantage of benefits offered by these new measures."
My private member's bill fits right into the comments of the Minister of National Revenue. Some small businesses could not meet the requirements of the government. They were only given 12 months to apply for a rebate. In keeping with the minister's perspective, I think we should have made it possible for small businesses to apply for their rebate at least for another year.
I have another comment in June 1992 by the Minister of National Revenue. It is a press release as well, and I will quote from it:
"Many of the improvements have been made possible through new technology, which has been a cornerstone in our ongoing effort to increase competitive opportunities for business and to improve and simplify service to all taxpayers" -
Again a lot of the companies I am familiar with that missed out on the inventory rebate were doing the kinds of things the minister was suggesting: getting more modem, getting more technology, getting more up to date. In doing that they discovered that in some cases they were ineligible for the rebate on their inventory.
If this bill were in isolation, if this bill said: "We are going to extend from one year to two years the returns that are eligible, and nowhere else in the system can you qualify for a rebate after more than one year", I could understand the government not being in favour of this kind of legislation. It would be a fundamental change. The fact of the matter is the change is in this legislation.
Look at some of the other legislation people take advantage of in Canada, for example the tax fairness package mentioned by the Minister of National Revenue. If someone is eligible for a refund on income tax and for some reason has missed a deduction, a credit, or simply has not filed, that person is eligible for a rebate going back to 1985. Some seven years in back taxes can be claimed if you are eligible for a rebate.
On the income tax side, businesses can file for three years back for their income tax return and be eligible for a refund of the income tax they owe simply by filing. They have three years to do this.
If a business pays excise tax in excess of what it should and in doing its auditing checks its accounts and discovers it has overpaid its excise tax, it can file for a rebate of that extra payment. It has two years in which to file a claim.
In fact, in the GST legislation if a business finds at the end of a year that it has overpaid the amount of GST or has not claimed back the credits it is eligible for, it can claim those credits as the legislation allows back four years. I appreciate the legislation is not four years old, but as this legislation improves or as it extends in time all businesses will be eligible for a rebate of the credits on
March 29, 1993

GST for up to four years. Yet for some reason we have put in place a one-year limitation on the FST rebate.
My private member's bill changes that limitation from one year to two. Some might argue that we should go back three or four years, and certainly I do not have a problem with that based on the other record. It seems to me that the businesses with which I have had contact have missed the opportunity to claim the refunds.
My private member's bill is really quite simple. It does that. It allows businesses, basically small businesses, to go back for another year to claim a rebate on the inventory that they have truly paid for, that they can verify under all the rules and procedures that have taken place.
I hope that members will speak in support of this piece of legislation. Unfortunately I believe it will not be coming to a vote. Nonetheless the merits of the legislation are really very straightforward and I hope that all members of this House will see fit to support it.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity to speak on Bill C-363. I support the idea that the rebate period should be extended on the manufacturers' sales tax, or the inventory portion of the FST.
I have to use this bill to illustrate again that the GST is a poorly designed tax. It is a poorly designed tax and this bill further demonstrates the point, because we are adding a further paper burden on small business.
I compliment the hon. member on the notion. It should be a standard procedure. I do not know why he does not go with the normal three years as people were converting from the old tax to the GST, which to this day I do not support. It created red tape and it made bureaucrats out of most of the small businesses in this country.
This is another example of where the government did not really realize the difficulties that small businesses have to cope with.
The hon. member kept talking about the Minister of National Revenue talking about tax fairness. Last week the deputy minister of revenue appeared before the public accounts committee. He talked about the fact that the gross GST revenue is somewhere in the neighbour-
Private Members' Business
hood of $30 billion but after the credits, the costs and the conversion from the old tax to the new tax there is approximately $15 billion in net revenue. That is what the net is on the GST.
The Department of National Revenue has no cost benefit analysis of the GST. The Department of National Revenue has no sectoral analysis of the GST; in other words how much money was taken in from the tourism sector in this country before the GST and after the GST or how much money was collected in terms of general revenue in the retail industry before the GST and after the GST.
I want to talk about the cost to small business. The Department of National Revenue mentioned in committee that the departmental work cost $150 per registrant. That is what it cost the Treasury for the 1.6 million registrants.
However it has done absolutely no analysis of what it cost small business. We have a bill this morning in which a respected member on the finance committee is recognizing the paper burden, the added work that is taken on because of the transfer and the GST.
I would not be surprised if the cost of the GST to small businesses was somewhere in the neighbourhood of $1,500 to $2,500 per business a year. I do not think that is an unreasonable cost.
If we multiply that cost by the 1.6 million registrants it would mean that there is effectively no net positive take from the GST. The GST has really been a big loser.
The bill this morning further illustrates that the design of the GST was not a good one. When they were taking into account all the transfer conditions and difficulties they should have understood that small businesses would not immediately understand all the complexities of the GST and would not understand all the forms and rebate mechanisms.
I also have had many small businesses in my riding- and when I say many I mean four or five-come to me in the last four to five months on this issue. With the GST they have to take on added accounting responsibility and their accountants have discovered that they have been short-changed on the rebate mechanism from their inventory.

March 29, 1993

The department right now is not honouring them. It is saying that they are beyond the one-year period of eligibility for the rebate. Needless to say, when we have an economy such as we have today our small businesses are having a heck of a time getting cash, especially from the banks.
I still have not seen anything from the government on advertising the Small Businesses Loans Act. The minister said last Thursday when it received royal assent that we would see something immediately, but I have not seen anything yet.
However here is another example where the government has at least had a bit of a deathbed conversion in the sense that it is recognizing that there are a lot of small businesses that missed the opportunity because of the complexity of the GST in converting from the FST and converting their inventory into the new mode.
I compliment the member for catching this. It is very important that we correct it. I cannot wait for the day when we can deliver to Canadians a system that is simple, fair and efficient. The government has designed a tax, the GST, from which the gross revenues are $30 billion and the net revenues are $15 billion. That is before a cost on the underground economy which is estimated to be somewhere in the neighbourhood of $20 billion to $30 billion.
That is not counting the cost of the damage it has done to the general lack of confidence in the country which has exacerbated the unemployment insurance and welfare conditions in this country. It is not including the fact that individual businesses must incur added costs as a result of the GST process.
When we figure all these things in my calculations show that the GST is the biggest loser in terms of a tax that has ever been perpetrated on this country. I cannot wait for the day when that GST is just washed away.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on Bill C-363. My party and I are pleased to support the member's amendment to the Excise Tax Act to ensure that there is a better break for small business. The small business community was caught somewhat short when the GST was brought in.
In his remarks the member pointed out quite well that it was the small business community, those who often do their own books or have to hire an accountant to do books, that had missed out on deadlines with respect to the inventory rebate. It is important we ensure that the small business community is given all the advantages it can be given in this time when we in Canada are looking for the small business community to lead the recovery after the long and deep recession we have been in.
The member has pointed out in this particular amendment, on the back of the bill we spoke to the week before last on more amendments to the GST, and there were almost 300 amendments to the GST bill in that particular bill, that there are many problems with the goods and services tax. These problems are starting to raise their heads. Perhaps they had not been thought of and should have been thought of through a more in-depth look at where this bill was going.
The cost of this particular legislation to the small business community has been devastating. While the member for Broadview-Greenwood has pointed out that there have been no studies done by Revenue Canada with respect to the cost to the small business community, a recent survey conducted in the past year by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business of its members pointed out that the cost to small business has been excessive.
If we are to continue with this foolish goods and services tax that over 82 per cent of all Canadians said they did not want and still do not care for, we have to look at the cost of administration to the small business community. Right now in almost every province the small business community gets an administrative fee back from the collection of the provincial sales tax.
In the case of the goods and services tax the burden of the administration of this horrible tax falls on the small business entrepreneur himself or herself. That cost is substantial. The cost to the small business community is not just in the administration of that tax but also in the fact that in border communities people go cross-border shopping to get their goods and services where they do not have to pay tax.
Recent studies done in my riding and in other parts of Canada by various organizations have shown that it is the taxation level that has to a great extent caused people to

go across the border to shop. The burden of the added 7 per cent goods and services tax has been one that people simply are not willing to pay anymore. A study done in my riding showed that the majority of people going across the border were doing so to escape the goods and services tax.
This has fallen off substantially over the last little while because of the dropping exchange rate. It is a positive step to ensure that the exchange rate is lower. It helps our communities along the border to ensure they remain competitive among the people who would normally shop there.
The member for Broadview-Greenwood commented with respect to the public accounts committee on which I sit how in discussing the administration of the goods and services tax people in our ridings and across Canada often ask what has been collected and how much of this money is going toward debt reduction. From looking at the public accounts and speaking to the officials of Revenue Canada it appears that over $29 billion has been collected from the goods and services tax. Of that amount over $14 billion has been returned in rebates of various kinds and natures, bringing the level down to something in the area of $15.3 billion that is netted out.
Revenue Canada officials tell us that net does not take into consideration the administration costs for the government, so we are looking below the $15 billion mark; in other words approximately a 50 per cent recovery for the amount that we are collecting from the people of Canada on the goods and services tax.
It is not a very efficient tax. It has been pointed out that there are 400,000 small businesses that did not have to register for this, businesses with under $30,000 a year in gross revenues, that in fact have applied. There are various reasons why the small business community may want to apply to ensure that it gets tax rebates for major capital expenditures, but for the most part it appears that these people could be weeded out with a proper push by the Revenue Canada taxation people to ensure that they understand exactly what the tax is all about and whether in fact it is to their advantage.
Private Members' Business
In talking to a number of community organizations throughout the province of British Columbia, a number of them registered for the goods and services tax because they felt they had to do it. The misunderstanding of community organizations was with businesses grossing under $30,000 and in most cases not having major capital expenditures where they would be getting rebates.
This is a burden to not only them in filing but also to Revenue Canada taxation. I think we also have to look at that area of the goods and services tax to try to get the numbers of people who have registered down and get the efficiency rate of Revenue Canada up.
Over all I think we have recognized that the small business community is the community to lead us out of the recession. The government has taken steps toward this in the Small Businesses Loans Act, but I think the government must also look at the devastation that it has wreaked upon the small business community with legislation like the goods and services tax at a time when the government was warned that we were heading into a recession and that the goods and services tax coming on stream when it did would cause nothing but devastation, would increase the inflation rate, and would cause problems for the small business community with people not wanting to purchase from it. I think that has proven correct.
We have to look at what we should do in place of the goods and services tax to kick-start the economy with the small business community. We have to bring in fair taxation where all Canadians are treated on an equal basis of fairness. We have to look at a phase-out of the goods and services tax starting first of all with things like books. They should never have been taxed in the first place. Placing taxation on education is simply unbelievable. It was stupid at the time and it is stupid now.
I would suggest that with a proper phase-out of this tax we can bring in tax fairness to all Canadians, a tax that is progressive, not regressive, and ensure that the Canadian people get back on track, that the unemployment rate of over 11 per cent is dropped substantially to single digit numbers and that all people in Canada feel they are part of the Canadian economy and part of the recovery.

March 29, 1993
Private Members' Business
We have to go one step further than this member has gone in ensuring that the small business community has the opportunity of getting rebates by doing away with the tax totally.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to comment on the bill introduced by the hon. member for Ontario. On January 1, 1991 the new legislation on the GST came into effect. At the time, our government allowed businesses with inventories on which they had paid the manufacturers' sales tax a period of 12 months starting January 1,1991 to file for the rebate which could then be passed on to the consumer.
I am referring to all businesses registered with Revenue Canada at the time that had already paid the tax. As a result of these claims the government paid out $2.5 billion in rebates. The government felt that during this 12-month period businesses had been given ample time to file their claims considering that the purpose was to enable businesses to pass on the savings to potential customers.
If today the government were to extend the deadline beyond December 31, 1991 I do not think that purpose would be served. I doubt the few businesses that failed, for whatever reason, to file for their rebate would pass the savings on to consumers who purchased the goods during the past 24 months. And that is not what the government intended.
The rebate was suppose to have the effect of reducing the price of certain goods, and that is exactly what happened. Finance Canada said when we were arguing in favour of the GST that there would certainly be a 1.25 per cent increase in consumer prices once the GST was put in place and, as you know, this included services. However, as a result of the business inventory rebates the increase was not 1.25 per cent but 1.1 per cent, an advantage for the consumer.
That was one of the benefits of the GST and I take credit for qualifying the government's position on proposals for changes. I would also like to mention that the GST has had a positive impact on exports of Canadian products to foreign markets. Before the GST was introduced the tax component of our exports was as much as 13 per cent. After the GST was introduced Canadian exporters, according to the Canadian Manufacturers Association, had a competitive edge equal to 1.6 per cent of their total sales. The result has been better penetration of foreign markets. This is one of the major advantages of the GST which is also responsible for increased sales of manufactured products to the United States since 1989-90 and during the present decade.
The same applies to capital equipment costs which are major inputs that must be recouped by Canadian manufacturers. The Canadian Manufacturers Association claims that the price of equipment used to manufacture products has gone down 4 per cent as a result of the GST. That 4 per cent represents $3.5 billion.
Retailers have confirmed that the price of most of the products they sell has gone down as a result of the GST. Because of the positive impact of the GST Canada's total GNP for one year increased by $9 billion, which means about 60,000 new jobs. According to an article in the Toronto Star of December 31, 1992-a newspaper that can hardly be accused of supporting the government's policies-even the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, which speaks for small business and fought the new tax tooth and nail, is starting to get used to the idea of a new tax system in Ottawa. The Federation says its members have spent millions of dollars to put the GST in place and are not prepared to accept any more changes.
It was also said that the GST would be an inexhaustible source of new money for the government and that was one reason why people should object to the tax. That is not the case. The GST has raised about 15 or 16 billion dollars annually, even less than anticipated. We are not seeing phenomenal amounts flowing into the Treasury as a result of collecting the GST.
Mr. Speaker, I will conclude my remarks with a comment from the Free Press of February 13, 1993, which says that although it is not perfect the GST is about the best tax we could have. It is visible. It is hard to evade. Even millionaires and their lawyers have to pay 7 per cent more on all goods and services. People said the GST would penalize the little man but the opposite is true. The GST penalizes on the basis of what you buy, and
March 29, 1993

since the wealthy buy more they will pay the lion's share of the GST.
For all these reasons I believe it would be inappropriate to make these changes and focus the energies of an increasingly expensive bureaucracy on a new accommodation for the sake of a few businesses that had 12 months to take advantage of the opportunity given them by the government to file their claims. That is why I recommend the status quo.

Mr. Speaker, this whole matter of the rebate under the goods and service tax was discussed in the finance committee hearings during 1989. It would have been discussed more fully had the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party not boycotted the hearings dealing with the bill.
The boycott by the member for Okanagan-Similka-meen-Merritt indicates the attitude that created all sorts of problems in this legislation. The reason we need the changes we now have before the House in legislation is that we could have done a better job in putting the bill through had members on the opposite side of this House put their minds to the whole matter.
Shame.

The member of Okanagan-Similka-meen-Merritt is now saying "Shame". He is the member who came to committee meetings but did not do much in the way of input.
With the goods and services tax we changed one consumption tax for another. The new consumption tax called the goods and services tax came into effect on January 1, 1991. Prior to that all goods in the hands of retailers bore some degree of federal sales tax. It was difficult to determine what the federal sales tax was.
Some people bought from a wholesaler; some people bought directly from the manufacturer; and some people bought from a company that imported goods into Canada. In some cases the goods went through two or three hands before they came to the retailer. The goods were all taxed originally at the manufacturers' gates at 13.5 per cent by and large, but what the amount of the manufacturers' tax was on the shelf of a retailer was difficult to determine. After a great deal of discussion
Private Members' Business
the government came to the view that 8.1 per cent of the gross inventory of a retailer could be said to represent the former manufacturers' sales tax. That was the rule of thumb.
In some cases there was substantially less tax. In other cases there was substantially more tax. In order to be fair in transferring the system, in moving from one system of taxation to another system of taxation, business people were given a year if they wanted to claim on a deduction basis, from their monthly or quarterly tax remittances 8.1 per cent of their inventory held for sale. Businesses were also given $1,000 to set up their books.
My friend speaks of businesses that did not bother doing all that. They should have done it, but they did not do it. The question is: How long should the system of government stay open to look after people who do not do what they are required under the law to do?
Remember this is a one-shot matter. This is not like failing to file income tax, not paying taxes on time, or not doing something on time where there will be penalties and so on, something that can still be done. This is a situation of determining what is the final amount one should get back, deducted from inventory, and inventory ought to be available for it to be proven.
When someone comes in a year later and makes a claim, how do we audit the inventory? How do we go back to check whether the claim is correct? What kind of staff is the government supposed to have, to keep on tap to look after problems that develop a year later or over a year later?
The problem is that when changing from one system to another we need fixed rules as to when the change takes place. The matter was discussed in the committee I chaired of making recommendations concerning the report of the government or working out the goods and services tax in the first place.
At one point the government's view was that it should not give any rebate at all, that the tax should be imposed and the old buried manufacturers' tax would stay in the system and we would not bother giving any rebate at all. We felt in committee that was unfair, that people ought to get a rebate, and the matter was argued out. The

March 29, 1993
Private Members' Business
member who is proposing the bill was on that committee. We argued it out.
We came up with a year. We came up with this system. It is a rough and ready system. It did give a rebate for those who filed but they had to file. They had to claim. They had to claim the $1,000 accounting claim too. They had to do a lot of other things. They had to get a number. If they did not do that, too bad. There was a lot of advertising. There were lots of public discussions. The papers were full of it. The opposition made sure the papers were full of it day after day.
It is surprising how people could say they did not hear about it or they did not know they had to do it a whole year after the goods and services tax came into place.
This is a very important tax system. It is a tax system that works exceptionally well. It is one of the great advantages in our economic system that is leading us out of our recession. It has made it possible for our businesses to be more than competitive with the Americans. It indicates why the American ways and means committee is now studying our tax system and will be using it.
Fifteen years from now.

It is too bad the member opposite does not understand the goods and services tax and how we do not add the cost of tax to our exports any longer or penalize people who manufacture in Canada any longer. But we do not. This system is working well.
I understand the desire of my colleague who has brought in Bill C-363 and the reason for the claim. However I have to say to him when changing over from one system to another there comes a time when one has to say: "That is it". Unfortunately that is it as the far as the one year is concerned.
Therefore, may I say that I do not believe we could accept the member's bill as a piece of legislation at this point. We have had a full two years of the goods and services tax. There have been very substantial rebates. The tax is in place and working well. It did not lead to the inflation that was suggested; indeed, that has been eliminated. After all, the rebate system was designed so that the money could be put back into the economy during 1991 when the change-over was taking place.
1992	is beyond the year period. By 1992 all of the inflation had been absorbed as a result of this tax and so the need for the rebate had also been absorbed.

Mr. Speaker, I will stop before the time runs out on this debate so that one of the government members no doubt will get up to talk and debate the bill out.
In reply to the point we just heard from the member for Mississauga South, it was a biscuit maker from Toronto who pointed out to me that the GST was going to have a significant impact on their export sales. I remind the member that the manufacturers' sales tax did not apply to exports before.
He might be interested in hearing how it was going to adversely affect the export sales of this biscuit manufacturer. In just a couple of sentences, it was believed that if the GST hit domestic biscuit sales the demand for biscuits would go down an estimated 15 per cent. This would mean cuts to staff, cuts to employment. Therefore the cost per export biscuit would go up significantly and would make their sales to the United States in this case less competitive. This would be as a direct result of the goods and services tax which those opposite always cite as being a panacea.
March 29, 1993

Government Orders

Let us have no more of this drivel that the GST helped our export sector. For those who may not know it on that side of the House, as I said before the manufacturers' sales tax never applied to exports.
Just to pick up on the point made by the member for Broadview-Greenwood, we understand the GST is now raising about $30 billion a year. There are about two million registrants. I think I can fairly say that my friend from Broadview-Greenwood knows the small business community better than anybody on that side of the House. He estimates that it costs about $3,000 per registrant for having the privilege of collecting the GST. If we deduct the credits, the family credits and the input credits, the revenues are about $15 billion. If we take off the other $3,000 times two million registrants that is about $6 billion. Basically, in terms of being useful to the economy, we get down to about $9 billion which this abomination is creating for our economy.
The hon. member mentioned the underground economy which has nourished under this. I bet that a good number of the members on that side of the House know people who live more and more through personal corporations. They buy cars for personal use. I know Revenue Canada does not like that. However, they have a personal corporation and can buy a car, use it for personal use and claim the import tax credit. However, most Canadians do not have personal corporations for one reason or another.
This tax is making it harder for fairness, which has never been a concern for members on the other side of the House.

['Mr. Speaker, from March 28 to April 18 the Body Shop retail chain will be conducting a national campaign to
combat child poverty. Its 105 stores will be displaying giant posters declaring that child poverty is a national disgrace. Their staff will be initiating letter-writing campaigns and encouraging community schools and city officials to become more involved in alleviating child poverty. In short, they will be devoting money and time to help reduce child poverty in Canada.
All of this comes at a time when the federal government has been busy looking at ways to redefine poverty rather than to solve it.
In 1984 over four million Canadians were living in poverty in this country and more than one million of them were children. According to the most recent statistics, still more than four million Canadians live in poverty and still more than one million of them are children.
The Body Shop is to be congratulated for its efforts to broaden awareness of poverty issues in Canada and for taking concrete action where the present government has only provided rhetoric.
This government should listen very carefully to this socially conscious business and act now to alleviate child poverty.']

speechtext:
Motion No. 1.
That Bill C-92 be amended in Clause 42

March 29, 1993
Government Orders
(a)	by striking out lines 41 to 48 at page 86, lines 1 to 45 at page 87, lines 1 to 48 at page 88, lines 1 to 15 and lines 39 to 47 at page 89, lines 1 to 45 at page 90, lines 1 to 47 at page 91, lines 1 to 47 at page 92, lines 1 to 50 at page 93, lines 1 to 48 at page 94 and lines 1 to 22 at page 95; and

\ English]
She said; Mr. Speaker, I move this motion which deals with clause 42 of Bill C-92. It has to do with the 21-year rule on private trusts.
I was very careful to allow the part of the amendments to private trusts to stand. It is very important that the private trusts not be allowed to be refreshed so that the extension of the rules will not be allowed to go on in perpetuity.
On the other hand, it is very important that we keep the 21 years. One of the reasons it was put in place back in 1972 was definitely to ensure that at some point family trusts which had been set up would be subject to capital gains taxation. This was a way of deciding at what point the assets would be valued and capital gains taxation would apply.
The government was trying in many ways to remove this 21-year rule in committee. I studied it very closely. I became more and more convinced that in effect the government was trying to give a break to a class of wealthy Canadians. They certainly have already had a very good break on taxation by not paying any tax on substantial capital assets.
We know if the properties were to accede to the beneficiaries of the trusts they would not have to pay capital gains at this time. However many of these trusts were set up so that the parents could retain control. At the same time on their death no capital gains would be levied. In essence it would defer taxation on capital gains for a very long time; perhaps as long as 60, 70 or 80 years.
We believe that by removing the 21-year rule this is exactly what will happen. We do not think it is right. We think it is a massive tax loophole. In committee we were told there were other loopholes and we strongly believe
that all tax loopholes have to be closed. The fact that there are still some around does not justify keeping, extending or creating a better tax loophole. Therefore we are very much opposed to extending the 21-year rule.
In committee we asked many questions. We wanted facts and figures. The finance department told us it did not have any. I have a great deal of difficulty believing it is impossible to come up with ballpark figures on the amount of revenue the government is deferring indefinitely if it strikes down the 21-year rule.
We all know that whatever the finance department decides to do it generally has all the statistics and all the facts and figures and can go on ad infinitum with facts and figures to back up its argument. Suddenly, however, for some reason when it comes to this particular clause it claims to not have any information and is extremely vague. My only feeling is that the finance department has somehow decided not to look into it because the revenue implications would be quite horrendous.
I ask the government to consider who it really should be representing. Should it be a handful of wealthy family trusts or should it be the people of Canada?
I was in Hearst over the weekend to attend a nomination meeting for one of our Liberal MPs and I met many people. Somehow I know they would not understand why a clause such as this one or a move such as this one would be made when they are suffering the bulk of taxation. They are, by and large, the ones who have been subjected to the GST and the many increases the government has put forward.
I really take offence at seeing a minister of this government make fun of what I am saying here today. It just shows a type of insensitivity to Canadians, that somehow these people have forgotten whom they represent. Do they represent the average Canadian out there or do they represent a select few? I do not wonder; I know they have somehow forgotten. It is high time they were reminded.
I am pleased to see the hon. minister acting a little bit more seriously while we are discussing these kinds of tax loopholes.
When I was in committee the Conservatives talked about setting up these trusts because some of the beneficiaries were disabled. I want to say that these
March 29, 1993

trusts generally were not set up to look after disabled children. If a trust is set up to look after a disabled child one does not put in assets which appreciate so much as one puts in revenue generating types of instruments. This is so that the disabled person can have a good and adequate cash flow to keep them going.
At any rate, I know that if this government really wanted to look after disabled people it would not be worrying about this 21-year rule. It would be allowing these trusts to pay the capital gains on the appreciation of their assets. It would have substantial revenues whereby it could do things for some of the disabled people it pretends to be so interested in helping.
I fail to understand why the government is insistent on abolishing the 21-year rule. I want to ask every member of the House to consider the serious debt and deficit implications we have. After all the rhetoric we hear about dealing with the debt and the deficit, the government talks a great line, turns around and forgoes revenues at this time having to do with these trusts. These represent substantial amounts of revenue that would help address the problem of the debt and the deficit.
I can only ask once more for the government to allow my amendment to stand and to vote in favour of it so that the same people the government purports to want to help really can be helped. At the same time we would address the debt and the deficit. It is more than time that we stop just talking. We should actually do something about it. Closing this loophole would be a tremendous step.

Mr. Speaker, today we are addressing very serious legislation that exposes in many respects the priorities of government. I want to begin by saying that we are dealing with Bill C-92 which includes private family trust tax legislation.
To understand what we are doing we have to go back to the year 1972 when the Liberal government of the day introduced what is called the 21-year rule that required private family trusts be assessed capital gains after 21 years of the money being in family trusts. They would then pay tax on their increase in wealth at that time. In other words it was a method of deferring taxes on capital gains for 21 years.
Government Orders
We recognize that no capital gains tax has ever been levied under this 21-year rule and that all private family trusts that existed on or before 1972 would be subject to tax for the first time in January 1993. However, the government has introduced the legislation which we are debating now to eliminate the 21-year rule. It means that a trust set up today for a young child could go tax-free until the child dies, which could be 80 years from now. In other words it would defer the tax for up to 80 years in some cases.
What are we talking about here? What is an example of a family trust? Because of the privacy rules which we support naturally we do not have information on specific families or individuals. That is the way it should be. Available court records show the trust established by Samuel Bronfman for his daughter had a value in 1969 of $70 million.
Today that trust would have had a value of well over $600 million if it had been kept in very conservative investments for that length of time. What we are talking about here are massive amounts of money on which taxes are not paid until the end of this period. Any tax expert would tell us that this means taxes will not be paid, period.
I want to say what some professionals have said about the tax initiative raised by the government that we are debating today. Sidney Goldstein of Goldstein, Goldstein and Goldstein in Ottawa had this to say:
There is no question that it represents a massive windfall for existing trusts.
Kathryn Bush of Blake Cassels had this to say:
A cynical person might suggest that pressure from influential political supporters also should be listed as a reason for the draft legislation.
Neil Brooks, whom we all know, is the associate dean at Osgoode Hall Law School at York University. He had this to say:
The government has given Canada's wealthiest families notice that it intends to give them a gift worth several billion dollars.
Arthur Drache of Fraser and Beatty had this to say:
If legislation now before Parliament is not passed before the end of the year, thousands of trusts would be hit with massive tax bills.
It is helpful because a lot of us are not tax experts. We do not have degrees in tax law or belong to firms that are into estate tax planning and so on. We rely on experts

March 29, 1993
Government Orders
and that is why we have committees. I look across the aisle at one of my favourite politicians, the hon. member for Mississauga South. He sat in on a very important meeting of the finance committee a few weeks ago where experts were invited to speak.
One of the two experts, Mr. Neil Brooks, had this to say, and I am quoting from the transcript of the finance committee hearings:
First of all, this amendment will clearly result in a number of Canada's wealthy families paying less tax this year than they otherwise would. There just cannot be any question about that.
The amendment will allow Canada's wealthiest families to defer paying tax on their accrued capital gains substantially beyond what any other tax avoidance technique now permitted by the act allows them to do. This change will usher in a new era of tax planning by the use of persona] trusts to avoid the deemed disposition on death. Over time it will have substantial revenue consequences.
Instead of creating one more loophole by which people can avoid or defer the deemed disposition of capital gains on death, the government should be closing the existing loopholes. The act now contains a number of loopholes which allow a person to freeze the value of their property, but maintain control over it and avoid paying tax on gains that accrued while they controlled that property. The government should be closing the existing loopholes that permit estate freezing.
My final comment is that this amendment is bad tax policy because there is absolutely no theoretical tax justification for the amendment that is being proposed. It will only benefit high income
people.
Professor Neil Brooks was followed by Mr. Sidney Goldstein. He is the senior partner in Goldstein and Goldstein, Barristers and Solicitors, and acts as a tax adviser and planner to his clients. He had this to say:
Having said that and given the view that there was some affiliation with Tories, I too am questioning the appropriateness and purposes of this proposal.
In other words, he was saying that his usual dispensation is to be supportive of Conservative government initiatives as a friend of the government, but this was going too far to tax his comments that he simply could not speak positively about this initiative under any circumstances. He went on to say the following:
I endorse most of the comments Professor Brooks has made. Deferral is a very powerful and very valuable benefit. One of the arguments that has been made here and in various publications is that the proposal just shifts when the tax is going to be paid. Whether you pay it now or later, the same amount of tax is going to be paid, but that is not true.
In other words, the usual explanation is that while this is simply deferring when tax will be paid, here is one of the most senior tax advisers in Canada saying that is patently untrue. This is not a fact. Again, humble people like myself simply have to take advice from these experts. He goes on to say:
The proposal here, and I second Professor Brooks' comment, is more generous than any other proposal in the act. The deferral is until the last of a class of persons dies potentially. That is likely to be a significantly longer period of time than if each individual child received their own share directly and paid tax as each of them died, sold property or left the country.
In other words, he is just saying that here is the ultimate in tax loopholes and tax boondoggles. He goes on to say:
In my own practice and based on my professional contacts and various direct information-ignoring the speculation of what major estates in the country might benefit -the potential tax benefits from this proposal are in the millions of dollars. I do not act for the Desmarais, the Bronfmans or the Thomsons, but I do act for people who have substantial real estate holdings and substantial portfolios of publicly listed shares and they will benefit significantly from this proposal.
I could go on reading from the transcript of the finance committee hearings, but perhaps I will simply wrap up by saying that two of the most experienced and respected tax advisers in Canada have said this has to be the loophole of loopholes. This has to be the ultimate granting of a gift to those who need it least. This is a tax giveaway to the most wealthy families in Canada.
On the one hand the government is saying it has to charge GST on children's books and Bibles. On the other hand it is giving the wealthiest families the ultimate tax loophole. Does it not tell us a great deal about how our tax system has evolved? It is a mess. It is a disaster. It is the disaster of disasters.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to say the amendment of the hon. member for Sudbury has some advantages in that it does not totally wipe out the tightening of the system concerning trusts.
The current act is so full of loopholes that it enables a trust to continue to roll over and over. Just by simply changing the trustees under the existing statute the 21-year period is revived. The government has settled that issue with people who have existing trusts by cutting
March 29, 1993

back on the deferral period to the deferral allowed for the first generation removed from the settlor and the tax applies on the death of the first generation.
Currently, because of the ability to roll it over and over with each succeeding change in trustees, the 21-year rule that is supposed to be a terrible rule that will prevent the government from collecting all sorts of money is a massive loophole for the wealthiest families, as my friend from Kamloops said. We have closed that massive loophole. I am at least pleased that the member for Sudbury has recognized the government's positive action in that regard.
We have made arrangements for these trusts to terminate when the youngest or the last person or whoever is immediately the beneficiary related to the first generation from the settlor dies.
There are two kinds of trusts. There are trusts set up in wills and most of the trusts that are dealt within this statute really are trusts set up by people who die. When they die the capital gains is paid on their assets and then their assets are put in trust for the beneficiaries. The trust can run until the death of the beneficiary if the beneficiary is one beneficiary removed from the testator and that is the end of it.
It does not require winding up a trust in a 21-year period but it allows the trust to run its normal course. That seems to me to be very fair. As I said, most of these things are put together by people in their wills. They are testamentary trusts.
Some trusts, however, are set up by people who want to do major inter vivos settlements. When a person does an inter vivos settlement he or she has to pay capital gains tax on all assets that have been put in trust. To the government that is a bonus because it gets its capital gains tax in advance when the settlor sets up the trust. The government does not have to wait until the settlor dies.
Some people suggest this is a great advantage to the settlor. I suppose an advantage is an advantage if it is perceived to be an advantage. It may not be an advantage at all because the settlor is paying tax to the government sooner than he or she would normally have to pay it. To the government that is an advantage. To the government the sooner a person pays tax the better, as pointed out by my friend from Kamloops. This might be perceived by some to be a great tax loophole but frankly on balance it
Government Orders
is no loophole at all. It is just the payment of tax perhaps earlier than the government might normally expect it.
I recommend this statute be left as is. We did not hear in committee, despite the evidence of Mr. Goldstein and Professor Neil Brooks, any real justification for changing it. The member for Sudbury who has made the amendment we are speaking to now recognizes the advantage of the changes proposed. I suggest we carry on recommending the advantages of all the changes rather than just being selective. I think the statute should pass as is and the amendment should be defeated.

Mr. Speaker, one of the problems the government does not seem to be recognizing is the perceived unfairness of the current tax act that exists in this country today. It is that perceived unfairness that is causing a great deal of difficulty.
There are many aspects of the tax regime which are not fair, but the perception is so much greater than the reality. It is that feeling or perception which is causing this malaise in attitude within our country that affects every aspect of a person's life. When people in a working environment do not feel they are being treated fairly it affects the quality of their work whether it is physical labour or creative work. The tax design of this country, the Income Thx Act, is one of the main culprits in causing this feeling that the system is not treating individuals fairly.
When people feel they are not being treated fairly it not only affects their work habits, but in the case of the Income Tax Act it causes a tremendous cash economy to develop. In 1985 the then Minister of National Revenue, the current Minister of Communications, said the underground economy at that time was close to $40 billion. He estimated-I am sure he got this advice from his officials in the Department of National Revenue-that the lost revenue to the Treasury on that underground economy was somewhere in the neighbourhood of $9 billion.
Today they say the underground economy is somewhere in the neighbourhood of $100 billion. If we use the minister's formula from that time we could say there is probably something in the neighbourhood of $15 billion to $18 billion in lost revenue to the Treasury because people feel they are not being treated fairly and the

March 29, 1993
Government Orders
underground economy, the cash economy, is exacerbated.
These trust funds are one of the prime reasons why people feel the current Income Tax Act is not a fair piece of legislation. When we have an Income Tkx Act where family trusts or trust funds have not had any tax burden over a 21-year period, how could anybody possibly think it is a fair system?
I realize this started off as a Liberal initiative. It has gone through successive regimes including nine years of a Conservative regime. It seems to me that they have a tremendous opportunity to do something special in tax reform, something that would cause people to think that even though they have been insensitive on the GST in the area of family trusts they have the courage to address a very tough issue.
The problem with the family trusts is that no one knows how much money is in those family trusts. We hear estimates ranging from $10 billion to $30 billion in trust funds that have been sitting around untaxed for 21 years. Now the government wants to extend it for an indefinite period of time.
I have been approaching the issue of comprehensive tax reform with a very specific idea, the single tax plan. Corporations and individuals would be taxed at a single rate of 20 per cent. After seniors, families with children and charitable organizations got their tax credit people would pay 20 per cent. Under the single tax system interest bearing amounts on these family trusts would be in the loop. It is an air-tight system. That is what Canadians want today. They want an air-tight system. They want a fair system. They want a system that is efficient. They want a system they can understand. More than anything they want a system where everyone is accountable.
This trust provision in the Income Tkx Act is wrong if for no other reason than there is absolutely no accountability. No one really knows how much money is in the trusts and how much money is being made. The fact it has gone on for 21 years without any accountability is wrong and I certainly think it needs to be amended.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak to the elements of the legislation that we are most concerned about in Bill C-92, and that is the whole question of the private family trust tax and the fact that the government has chosen to continue it for yet another period of time.
Changes to the legislation concerning taxation of private family trusts was first proposed by the Minister of Finance in draft legislation on February 11, 1991. Despite considerable criticism from the professional community, these technical amendments were introduced in draft legislation released in December 1991. Finally the legislation was brought to the House by notice of a ways and means motion June 19 last.
The legislation has been around for quite some time. We have been aware of it and have been watching it move through the process.
The current legislation which this seeks to amend covers private family trusts. It goes back 21 years to the 1972 tax reform brought in by the former Liberal government when the federal estate tax was eliminated and the capital gains tax introduced.
This change left a potentially enormous tax loophole. Capital gains taxes are levied only when gains are realized, usually when property is sold or at the time of death. Because trusts never die it means a private family trust could entirely escape paying taxes on assets held within the trust.
The Liberal government introduced a 21-year rule which required that private family trusts would be assessed capital gains after 21 years and pay tax on their increase in wealth. Clearly the government set the rules. It said for 21 years the trusts had a tax holiday but at the end of that they had to start paying their fair share.
Income tax is paid by the beneficiaries of the trust when property is distributed to them from the trust. No capital gains tax has ever been levied under this 21-year rule, and all private family trusts which had expired on and before 1972 would be subject to tax for the first time in January 1993.
Under this bill the government is proposing to essentially eliminate the 21-year rule. Trusts would be allowed to defer the 21-year rule until all the exempt beneficiaries have died. An exempt beneficiary can include a
March 29, 1993

child, spouse or parent of the trust settlor but not any individual of generations subsequent to that of the child. In other words no grandchildren.
This means that a trust set up for a young child today could go tax-free until that child died, which could be 80 years or more from now. It means the billions that are presently sheltered in private family trusts will not have to be subject to tax until the last exempt beneficiary dies.
This constitutes a tax loss of billions of dollars. While trusts will be allowed to accumulate wealth tax-free for many more decades, the government will be deprived of those revenues to reduce the debt and deficit, let alone the revenues necessary to improve lives of all other Canadians.
We do not know for sure how much is held in private family trusts. Almost no public information is available about the amount of wealth that is held in these trusts. Tax privacy laws which we support prevent Revenue Canada from providing information about any single trust and it does not provide any information about the aggregate amount of assets held in private trusts.
Sources within the financial industry have estimated the total value of assets held within trusts at $70 billion. This estimate seems fairly reasonable as it represents only 3 per cent of the $2.4 trillion total assets held by persons in unincorporated businesses in Canada.
How much revenue does the government lose from this particular change with the extension of the trust? It is difficult to estimate just how much tax revenue the government will lose but a very cautious estimate demonstrates what potential revenue is at stake. If only 1 per cent of the $70 billion in trusts was subject to tax next year a marginal tax rale of 30 per cent would raise over $200 million.
It is only fair that people who have these trusts are expected to contribute to the running of the country because that is really what it is all about.
I have a number of quotes from tax professionals. Sidney Goldstein of Goldstein, Goldstein and Goldstein in Ottawa says:
Government Orders
There is no question that it represents a massive windfall for existing trusts.
Kathryn Bush from Blake Cassels says:
A cynical person might suggest that pressure from influential -
You just read those.

I know and I thought they were so good I wanted to read them back into the record.
Let me start again. She said:
A cynical person might suggest that pressure from influential political supporters also should be listed as a reason for the draft legislation.
Again that was Kathryn Bush. Neil Brooks, someone who has been referred to in this House before and will be from time to time, said:
The government has given Canada's wealthiest families notice that it intends to give them a gift worth several billion dollars.
Finally Arthur Drache of Fraser and Beatty said:
If legislation now before Parliament is not passed before the end of the year, thousands of trusts could be hit with massive tax bills.
The government argues that these changes are necessary for a number of reasons. First, it has argued that the 21-year rule might interfere with trusts established by parents for the benefit of their disabled children.
The reality is that any trust set up for a disabled child will have annual allocations of the gains from that trust in order that the child may progress through school and through life. They would not be set up to provide a lump sum at some point in the future. Their needs do not get delayed for 21, 25 or 30 years. Their needs are now.
Any trust set up to ensure that the child of a wealthy person or a not so wealthy person is looked after financially will be designed in such a way that they would not require this particular rule.
As Sidney Goldstein argued:
If the government were really concerned about the needs of disabled kids, a better solution would have been to declare a special exemption for the disabled.
Second, the government has argued that unless the rules are changed some trusts may not be able to pay the taxes without the selling of assets, perhaps including a controlling block of shares in a private company. This

March 29, 1993
Government Orders
argument is probably the most valid of those offered by the government but it still makes little sense. Private trusts have had a full 21 years to plan for this tax, much more than ordinary taxpayers get.
One of the complaints we hear from time to time about governments of all stripes is that they change the rules. Here is a rule that has been in place for 21 years. Everybody knew what the rule was. A good financial planner would have considered that and have planned accordingly for the end of the 21-year rule this year.
Taxpayers in this situation could utilize the $500,000 small business capital gains exemption to avoid selling assets. The government also says that it is closing a loophole with this bill by preventing rollovers from one trust to another. It is true that a clause in this bill does close a potential loophole and we do support that, but it does not mean that the government has to create another massive loophole.
Although it may be onerous for the beneficiaries of some trusts to pay taxes in one shot after 21 years in capital gains, there is a provision to pay taxes from a 21-year deemed disposition in up to 10 annual instalments. That is in subsections 159(7) and 159(6.1) of the act. This will provide some relief for trust beneficiaries with modest incomes who do not wish to dispose of the assets at this time.
The law is clear. It provides some flexibility for those people who are not the wealthy family trust holders but of more modest means who perhaps could not afford to pay the kind of taxes that might be owed to the people of Canada.
In conclusion, this particular section of the bill indicates the reality of tax reform in Canada. It is tax reform for the very wealthy. It is tax oppression for the not so wealthy. That is why we in this party oppose the provisions in the extension of the 21-year rule. We want real tax reform which would ensure that those who have a lot of money begin to pay their fair share of running this country.

Mr. Speaker, I never thought I would have to rise here to protest against such a flagrant government bill. It is the worst fiscal injustice I have heard of since I have been in this House.
In recent years there have been all sorts of tax increases, especially the GST, which hit the middle class. All these taxes hit the middle class hard and today Bill C-92 would exempt family trusts. This means that the richest families in the land, those with the most money who enjoy the best that this world has to offer, would be exempted.
Twenty-one years ago the government here in this House decided that it would change the tax system. Taxes would not be collected on family trusts for 21 years, but after 21 years all gains on the family trusts would be taxed. Indeed in the past few years the great law firms in this country representing its wealthiest families have been putting pressure on the government to extend this 21-year exemption until the youngest children have died. This could be 20, 25, 30 or even 40 years in some cases.
How do we explain this change in attitude? Twenty-one years ago it was literally a gift to the wealthiest families with huge fortunes.
Now it wants to remove it. I have great difficulty understanding what inspired this change. Look at the situation our country is in with our middle class saddled with the heaviest tax load in the industrialized world. Still we are now dealing with a bill that would exempt the richest families in the land.
How can such a thing be justified? In committee we had experts like Neil Brooks, vice-dean of Osgoode Hall law school, with whom I spoke several times. He has a great reputation; he is a great tax expert who knows tax law. As you know, Mr. Speaker, I do not claim to be a tax expert, far from it, not when there are thousands and thousands of pages written on it. It is really complex and I for one am convinced that this law is deliberately complex.
For example, take the experts who appeared before the committee. They showed that it was indeed a gift, literally a huge tax break. But for whom? For the richest families in the country.
We have so much data clearly establishing that it is not justified. As you know, the richest families have the services of great experts available to them. They can put tremendous pressure on the government, for example through lobbyists here in Ottawa, to defend their cause. They can afford it. A middle-class person who earns his
March 29, 1993

Government Orders
daily living most definitely cannot afford the services of a tax expert. Earning his or her living takes all his time.
However, the wealthiest families in Canada enjoy advantages. I could quote figures; we do not know if hundreds of millions or billions of dollars could be saved in that way. At a time when we have an accumulated deficit of over $400 billion, we find a way to exempt the most fortunate class in our country. That is very strange and unjustified.
I hope Bill C-92 will raise many questions in Canada. The committee has already met, but I hope a great many people will start asking more and more questions as to why a government which has asked so much of the middle class would exempt the richest citizens. There is no justification for it.
The witnesses who appeared before the committee literally said that the government's arguments are phoney. There is no justification and these arguments are just stalling for time until they come to the House to pass the bill on third reading with their majority.
I know that on this side of the House the Liberal Party of Canada and the New Democratic Party will vote against it, that is sure. In a few months there could be a change of government, a hope I share with many Canadians. The Liberals will then form the government and we should rescind this bill which the present government wants to pass and tell the richest families in Canada: "You were exempt for 21 years. Now it's your turn to do your part. This country has been very generous to you; it is only right that you now pay your share".
I say to government members who cannot justify this bill that you will pay the price come election time. Canadians everywhere will ask: How can you justify Bill C-92 which exempts the richest families in the country? You have no justification. It is shameful.
I realize that we should always use parliamentary language, but you should be ashamed. If you are not ashamed, I wonder if we can expect the worst. I would like all those listening to the debates in this House to ask Conservative members the following question: How can you justify such a shameful measure?

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands - Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on this amendment to Bill C-92 as it pertains to the extension by the government of the 21-year rule for private trusts.
The context in which I would like to frame my remarks, which are in support of this Liberal amendment changing this piece of legislation, is that of ensuring that Canadians appear to pay and do pay their fair share of taxes. It is also in the context of the very real fiscal difficulties that we all know the federal government faces at the present time.
The decision by the government to extend the 21-year rule is one on which we are still being denied information that is necessary for us to have a full understanding of what exactly is involved. To many Canadians this decision appears to grant a very important loophole allowing the wealthiest in our society to continue to avoid paying tax on a very sizeable portion of their assets, namely their family trusts.
It is incumbent upon any government today that is serious about controlling expenditures and the deficit and that wants to ask Canadians to make a real sacrifice, as this government has done through the imposition of numerous and sizeable increases in taxation, to ensure that those in Canada who have sizeable assets are taxed appropriately on those assets, and in particular on the capital gains that accrue through the accumulation of those assets.
The 21-year rule was implemented 21 years ago to allow those families who fell into that situation a very long period of time to get their affairs in order and dispose of their assets. That 21-year period, in the opinion of members on this side of the House, was plenty of time for those families to deal with the business of financial planning.
This government has extended that period at a time when Canadians are generally feeling overburdened by taxes. There is a very strong suspicion afoot in this country that the wealthy do not pay their fair share of taxes and ordinary Canadians are being asked to assume, through increases in income taxes, through various forms of charges and through the GST, sizeable increases in

March 29, 1993

their tax burdens. It strains the credibility of any government when this is allowed to happen.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to stand in the House to speak at consideration of report stage of Bill C-92, an act to amend the Income Tax Act, the Canada Pension Plan, the Income Tax Conventions Interpretation Act and so on.
This omnibus bill includes numerous technical changes. There are quite a few areas of the bill that I definitely do agree with. There are some very positive aspects of it but there are two areas that I and my party disagree with.
We on this side of the House have put forward two amendments to Bill C-92. The first is a motion to amend clause 42 to remove the extension of the 21-year rule on private trusts and maintain present law. The second is a motion to amend clause 47 which is to remove the provisions that disqualify passive businesses from the capital gains exemption.
I will explain briefly what these two motions are about and why we are objecting to those two particular aspects of the bill.
The government's position is that it wishes to extend the 21-year rule because it wishes to remove the arbitrary nature of the 21-year figure. The government has tried to justify the extension of the 21-year rule for private trusts by emphasizing the plight of disabled children as the beneficiaries of these trusts. The government believes that this extension will not result in any forgoing of tax revenue. Therefore it sees this as a revenue neutral measure. Obviously we on this side of the House do not agree with the government on that analysis.
We heard testimony during the review of Bill C-92, more specifically with the 21-year rule on private trusts. Other members of this House have quoted Mr. Brooks and the five salient points he raised during the hearings. I would like to mention those too because I think they probably best summarize the main reasons as to why we are objecting to this clause in the bill.
The 21-year rule extension on private trusts will clearly result in a number of Canada's wealthiest families paying less tax this year than they otherwise would. Canada's wealthiest families will be able to defer paying tax on their accrued capital gains substantially beyond what any other tax avoidance technique now permitted by the act would allow them.
Instead of creating one more loophole by which people can avoid or defer the deemed disposition of capital gains on death, the government should be closing the existing loopholes that permit what is described in the trade as estate freezing. Not one reason the government has put forward for making this change holds any water.
The 21-year rule extension is bad tax policy in the sense that there is no theoretical tax justification. It will only benefit high income people. In addition, it is bad economic policy. It will in effect lock more investments into private trusts on which large capital gains will accrue. People will be reluctant to sell their investments even though they might indeed be bad investments because of the large tax liability that is accruing over time.
Those five points I just went through were made by an expert witness, Professor Neil Brooks, associate dean of Osgoode Hall Law School at York University. He is a tax lawyer and an estate planner. They were not made by someone who does not know what he is talking about. He is very familiar with the tax laws of this country and he is most concerned that this government would be moving in that direction.
I would like to move on to the Liberal Party's motion, the amendment to clause 47, to remove the provisions that disqualify passive businesses from capital gains exemptions.

This was a very generous arrangement. However that time has now passed. It is time these family trusts were paying taxes on those assets. These are not trusts for the poorest and the weakest in our society, but they are family trusts for the strongest and most powerful, the richest families in this country.

What we are dealing with here is the establishment of some new rules on the trusts. The loophole was created in 1972 by the Liberals. If a trust was created 21 years ago and some time between then and now to avoid the 21-year rule you wanted to transfer the trust from one management group or one trustee to another, simply creating a new trustee and a new trust exempted you of the 21-year rule and you had another 21 years to deal with it. Therefore, what we are doing is taking away that opportunity to simply roll the trust from one trustee to another thereby avoiding the capital gains.
Somehow there is this idea that this is a massive scheme to avoid capital gains tax by the rich. However, what I have not heard mentioned today is that if any person in Canada wanted to establish a trust the rules that go into this can include people who own cottages. I live in the greater Toronto region and I know there are lots of people who own cottages. They would like to put a cottage into a trust so that should something happen to them their children would have a system whereby they could share the ownership of the cottage for their generation. This piece of legislation is going to allow that to happen without families having to reach into their pockets 20 years from now to pay capital gains.
How does this happen? In order for an asset to be put into a trust an evaluation has to be put on the asset going into the trust. The person establishing the trust has to pay the capital gains tax on the assets that are being put into the trust. Therefore, if there is one million dollars in assets that one wants to put into a trust, one has them valued. One discovers that one bought them for $500,000, one has now valued them at $1 million and you put them into the trust. In order to put them into the trust one has to pay the capital gains tax on the $500,000 increase in value. Therefore there has not been an avoidance of tax. In fact it seems as if there has been a prepayment of tax because normally one would not have to pay the income tax on that capital gain until such time as one actually sold or disposed of the asset.
What is happening is that if somebody wants to put an asset into a trust they have to pay the capital gains accrued to date up front.
