It was just shifting it down the road for another 21 years.
Mr. Speaker, you have indicated my time is up. I frankly think with this type of provision going in as silently as it is today for the members who support it their time will be up if they do not watch out.

Mr. Speaker, this amendment has been moved to strike out the section of Bill C-92, which extends the 21-year rule for family trusts.
There is no question this is one of the most important pieces of legislation that will face this House of Commons this year. The extension of this family trust provision represents a colossal give-away to some of the wealthiest families in this country when the government
is talking about its deficit problems and claiming it has serious revenue difficulties.
Here we have something that hands out millions and millions of dollars to those who are already wealthy. This has no logic economically or in terms of fiscal management. If we thought there might have been some logic associated with it all we had to do was listen to the arguments of the Department of Finance and the assessment of those arguments, not from Neil Brooks but from Sidney Goldstein.
He noted at the start of his comments as a witness in committee that he was speaking as someone who had supported the Conservative Party, yet here is his assessment of what the Department of Finance had said: "The rationales given by the Department of Finance are very strained". He went on to say: "Many of the arguments presented relating to this proposal somehow don't hold water as soon as you look at them. There are other far simpler ways these problems could have been solved. There are other ways of drafting these proposals that would have resulted in a more limited impact. That leads to the question of why this proposal is being put forward in this fashion".
Mr. Goldstein is a man who works with people who frankly are trying to use the family trust provision to avoid paying tax. This is his assessment, honestly put to the people of Canada by somebody who has no partisan axe to grind, put as a Conservative testifying to this committee. I quote again from the committee testimony:
In my own practice and based on my professional contacts and various direct information -ignoring the speculation of what major estates in the country might benefit-the potential tax benefits from this proposal are in the millions of dollars. I do not act for the Desmarais, the Bronfmans or the Thomsons,
some of the large family holders of wealth in this country,
but I do act for people who have substantial real estate holdings and substantial portfolios of publicly listed shares, and they will benefit significantly from this proposal.
So much for the myth which the Conservatives are trying to put to us that this is simply a housekeeping measure to try to stop people from shifting from one 21-year trust to another 21-year trust. Here is an expert in the field who calls himself a Conservative and says
March 29, 1993

very clearly to the people of Canada that this is going to cost all of us as taxpayers millions of dollars.
We also saw testimony from Neil Brooks, one of the foremost tax experts in this country, to that same committee. I know my friend the former finance committee chairman has quarrelled with Mr. Brooks every time Mr. Brooks has appeared before the Finance Committee. I find it interesting, however, that my friend from Mississauga South did not say anything with respect to the comments of Mr. Goldstein. Those comments came from a Conservative. They came from somebody who deals in the area and they made it very clear that this particular provision is a waste of millions of dollars to the people of Canada.
Mr. Brooks went somewhat further. He said and I quote his final comment:
This amendment is bad tax policy because there is absolutely no
theoretical tax justification for the amendment that is being proposed.
It will only benefit high-income people.
In other words, there is nothing here that is going to help growth in the country. There is nothing that is going to lead to extra jobs for people in Canada. There is nothing that is going to create greater fairness in the burden of taxation for people across this country. Instead, this is the extension of a give away which the Liberal Party started. It is now being extended so grossly that it will give millions of dollars of extra benefits to some of the wealthiest families and some of the families who are simply wealthy in this country.
Why did things like this happen? Why should such a piece of legislation be brought before the House of Commons? The tax system is messed up badly and as we who talk to our constituents know it has increasingly hit middle income, working income people. Instead of correcting those problems in our tax system the government is bringing forward a set of proposals to help those people at the very top whose share of national market income in this country in the last six years under this Conservative government has gone up from 23 per cent to 26 per cent. They are already very wealthy. They have already received tremendous tax breaks and the government is giving them more tax breaks.
I am afraid there is something fundamentally rotten at the heart of our political system that it gives tax benefits
Government Orders
to those who are wealthy instead of those who really need them. It concentrates the benefits at the top instead of among middle income, working Canadians who are so hard pressed.
The people on the Conservative side must surely now recognize it is time to change such an unfair, rotten, unjust approach and withdraw this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, this party is going to oppose Bill C-92. There are things in it which we agree with but we disagree with the part of the bill we are talking about now.
Bill C-92 is a measure of a government that believes Parliament should not help the weakest members of society do better but make life easier for the richest members of Canadian society. We should perhaps call it the comfort bill for family trust holders in Forest Hill Village, Rosedale, Upper Westmount, Park Lane Circle and perhaps parts of Shaughnessy in Vancouver. Sony, I forgot the British Properties.
We believe the government is being deceitful by including this change in an omnibus bill which includes measures we support. The vast majority of our fellow citizens are subjected to an inheritance tax in the form of a deemed capital gains tax on death. There is no reason why those very few Canadians who are fortunate enough to have family trusts should have preferential treatment.
Those Canadians who are fortunate enough to take advantage of the 21-year rule were given 21 years to get their affairs in order, I put through you Mr. Speaker to the member for Mississauga South. Was it not enough time? There is no reason to extend what was more than generous deadline. Of course extending the 21-year rule is unfair to all of those who do not have family trusts.
We heard a lot this morning about Neil Brooks and what he said. He basically raised five points to the committee. The 21-year extension on private trusts will clearly result in a number of Canada's wealthiest families paying less tax this year than they otherwise would.
Second, Canada's wealthiest families will be able to defer paying tax on their accrued capital gains substantially beyond what other tax avoidance techniques now permit and the act would allow them to defer paying tax on capital gains.

March 29, 1993
Third, instead of creating one more loophole by which people can avoid or defer the deemed disposition of capital gains on death, this horrible government should be closing existing loopholes that permit what is described in the trade as estate freezing.
Fourth, the government has not put one reason forward as to why making this change holds any water.
Fifth, said tax expert Neil Brooks, the 21-year extension is bad tax policy in the sense that there is no theoretical tax justification. It will only benefit high-income Canadians.
In addition, this bad economic policy will in effect lock more investments into private trusts in which large capital gains will accrue. People will be reluctant to sell their investments even though they might be bad investments because of the large tax liability that is accruing over time.

I regret 1 must interrupt the hon. member.
It being two o'clock p.m., pursuant to Standing Order 30(5) the House will now proceed to statements by members, pursuant to Standing Order 31.

Mr. Speaker, this government has just passed new legislation that will encourage banks to increase their participation in small business financing.
This bill, which will make it more enticing to lend to small businesses, includes an increased ceiling on loan size from $100,000 to $250,000.
As well, businesses with yearly sales of $5 million will be eligible to apply, as opposed to the previous limit of $2 million. Even better, the federal loan guarantee has now been raised from 85 per cent to 90 per cent. A new addition of a retroactivity clause will make it possible for owners of small businesses to apply for loans six months after making a purchase.
Once again this government is taking positive steps to encourage entrepreneurship. I am hopeful that the banks will recognize these efforts and participate fully in this respect.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to bring to the attention of this House the plight of the people in the Annapolis basin area who are seeing their way of life threatened by actions of the minister responsible for ACOA.
The minister gave an ACOA grant without seeking any input from the people who already use the Annapolis basin: the clam diggers, the scallopers, the ground fishermen, the weir fishermen, the lobster fishermen, and the rockweed workers. These people do not need aquaculture, they need policies that will protect the existing industries in the Annapolis basin.
The minister obviously listens to the provincial minister of tourism when there are grants to be given out in Annapolis West, as was seen with the rock quarry and now with the announcement of a grant for aquaculture.
Giving out grants without knowing the effects shows the total disregard this Tory government has for the existing rights of those who live and fish in that area.
I call on the minister responsible for ACOA to put on hold the grant for aquaculture until public hearings have been held to determine the effect of such a grant on those people who earn their living from the Annapolis basin.

Mr. Speaker, the construction association of Prince Edward Island has joined the growing number of people and organizations urging the government to meet the requirements of the recent court decision regarding the fixed link and then begin construction without delay.
The association points out that a full 80 per cent of its workers, 3,700 people, are currently out of work with little hope for the future.
March 29, 1993

Islanders for a Better Tomorrow, another group representing business, labour, industry and the views of a clear majority of Prince Edward Islanders, has said: "Our main industries, our businesses, our working people, our unemployed and our children cannot afford to have this opportunity slip away due to the misguided efforts of a small and dwindling minority. Their supposed concern for the environment has proven to be selective and opportunistic. Decisive leadership and immediate action is therefore required on this project by the Minister of Public Works and the Parliament of Canada".
I once again add my voice to this call for action to proceed with this project which is extremely important to all of Atlantic Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am proud to announce that tomorrow, Tuesday, March 30, is Magic Tuesday in my riding of Broadview-Greenwood. On Magic Tuesday all the proceeds from food sales in local restaurants go to the Children's Wish Foundation, a foundation that looks after kids who are terminally ill.
Tomorrow if people are in Toronto or are going through on a business or tourism trip they should go to the Danforth and go to either the Astoria Shish Kebob House, the Athenian Garden, the Ilissia, Mr. Greek, Omonia, Ouzeri, the Palace Restaurant on Pape, the Pappas Grill, the Patris Dining Lounge, or Philoxenia. All of the great Greek restaurants in Toronto welcome people on Magic Tuesday.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to commend the government on its progressive attitudes toward regional development.
It was only three weeks ago that I rose to voice my concerns about the direction the Community Futures Program was taking. As a result of a meeting between the Minister of Employment and Immigration and representatives of the Triple S group from Selkirk I can tell the House that cause for concern has changed. The minister listened to a fair and balanced presentation
which has resulted in continued funding for the Triple S community futures group.
As I said in the beginning, I commend the government for funding success and working to eliminate failure.

Mr. Speaker, almost five years ago the Minister of Agriculture closed the border to imports of American honey-bees.
This move was a surprise for many bee keepers who had relied upon imports of queens and starter colonies from California on an annual basis. The varroa mite and the tracheal mite were found in U.S. bees. As they had not existed in Canada to that date the closing made sense. Chemical control is being used in the United States but mites have since found their way into several regions of Canada.
The border closure order is in effect until this fall, which is too late for next year's planning. Bee keepers need to know now what the government's intention is. Will the border be allowed to open when the five-year closure order dies this fall or will the ministry extend the order to keep it closed?
The futures of jobs and a competitive honey industry in 1994 depend on an early decision.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House to address the problem facing women who are persistently harassed, intimidated and threatened by men.
Men who are former partners or social friends sometimes pester or threaten women to the point where they become confined to their homes in fear of the harassment that awaits them when they go about their daily lives.
Over half of the states in the U.S. have laws giving police a tool with which to lay serious charges against anyone whose pattern of harassment poses a credible threat of physical or psychological harm.

March 29, 1993
Police officers who deal directly with persons involved in stalking incidents throughout the U.S. and Canada support such legislation because it gives them a more effective tool with which to protect women.
I think it important to note that this is an issue that overwhelmingly affects women. I understand that the Minister of Justice is considering a number of legislative options. I urge him and the government to act quickly and address the issue of stalking before the problem increases.

Mr. Speaker, management and factory workers at the Nestle plant in Chesterville are currently involved in a legal lock-out.
Last Thursday workers rejected a contract offer from the company which included a proposed continental work week. On Saturday the company implemented a lock-out.
As negotiations have currently ceased, management and labour are now faced with a situation which may impact on the future viability of the plant which employs 220 people in this community of 1,500 people.
Seventy per cent of the plant's production is exported to the U.S., and various economic pressures are being placed upon the plant to remain competitive in the U.S. marketplace and maintain its presence in Chesterville.
It is hoped that the management and workers at Nestle's Chesterville plant will be able to reach a mutually acceptable resolution to this dispute at the earliest opportunity.
* * #

Mr. Speaker, the whole concept of the environmental panel review of major national programs is on the line because of the refusal of the Government of Canada, particularly the Minister of Transport, to follow the decision of the environmental review panel dealing with the Pearson airport expansion.
That environmental review panel rejected the government's view concerning the location of the north-south runway and the extent of that runway. Notwithstanding
the total rejection of the government's proposal, the Minister of Transport has decided to proceed with the government's proposal in the government's way.
If the government is going to put the country to the expense of environmental review programs then the government has an obligation to follow through on them. If the environmental review panels will only be followed if they suit the government then the whole concept of the environmental review process is a ridiculous waste of taxpayers' money.

Mr. Speaker, almost nine years ago the Prime Minister said the words that will haunt him to his grave. He said the Conservatives believed that Canada's social programs were a sacred trust.
Eight years later, Canadians have witnessed an unparalleled assault on the social programs by this government, on every front. The Tories went on a search and destroy mission. They whittled away at everything from medicare to unemployment insurance and penalized the poor, the weak and the sick.
We know where the PM, that is the puppet master, stands. But where does his hand-picked successor stand on Canada's social programs?
The Minister of National Defence told journalists on the weekend, and I quote: "It is time to recognize that we must target our social services". What does that mean? Which programs does the minister plan to target?
For the past four years she sat at the cabinet table cheering on the GST, the Mulroney trade deal and the de-Confederation of Canada. The minister is for multi-billion-dollar cold war attack helicopters and against our social programs. That is her sacred trust, and it is a disgrace.

Mr. Speaker, during the government's consultation on the prosperity initiative one subject that came up many times was the need to
March 29, 1993

reconcile our educational system with a rapidly changing world.
One man in Red Deer is already grappling with this problem. Dr. Joe Freedman became involved in the educational system the way many of us do, as a concerned parent, but his concern about the quality of education prompted him to go one step further and undertake a comprehensive study of the Canadian educational system.
Dr. Freedman's report, entitled "Failing Grades", reviews major studies in the field of education. His conclusion is that Canadian students perform poorly in comparison with students in other industrial nations. He says that part of the solution is national co-ordination of educational policy.
Dr. Freedman's report deserves a serious second look. He has sent his video and report free of charge to every school superintendent in the country. Hopefully, they will receive it in the spirit in which it was delivered, as the work of a concerned parent who wants what is best for our country and its children.

Mr. Speaker, last weekend at Laurentian University there was general consensus among economic experts that the government has its fundamentals all wrong.
Pierre Fortin from the Universite de Quebec a Montreal charged that through its pursuit of zero inflation the Bank of Canada has driven the dollar too high so that foreign investors demand compensation in the form of higher interest rates.
John Smithin from York University said: "Experience seems to show that the economic slow-downs required to reduce inflation to a very low figure are much more severe and long-lasting, particularly in their impact on unemployment, than the public was originally led to believe".
Lars Osberg from Dalhousie blamed the Bank of Canada for costing the Canadian economy $70 billion per year with its pursuit of zero inflation.
When will this government leave this path of economic destruction and look seriously at the full employment solutions proposed by the New Democratic Party?

Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister Responsible for the Status of Women recently announced that as a result of a Canadian initiative the United Nations Commission on the Status of Women adopted the "Declaration on the Elimination of Violence Against Women".
The declaration states that violence against women impedes women's enjoyment of human rights and fundamental freedoms and calls on governments to exercise due diligence to prevent and punish acts of violence, whether perpetrated by the state, within the general community or within the home.
At the United Nations several delegations praised Canada's recent adoption of guidelines on women refugee claimants fearing gender-related persecution. These guidelines are the first of their kind in the world.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1988 the Minister of State for Multicultural-ism and Citizenship indicated his willingness to negotiate with Canada's Ukrainian community for redress of its claims arising from internment during World War I.
To date, the minister and his cabinet colleagues have procrastinated and delayed, notwithstanding the adoption of a resolution by this House urging action by the government. Today Mary Haskett is in Ottawa. She is the last survivor of the Spirit Lake Internment Camp in Banff National Park.
She has written an open letter to the Prime Minister and I quote from it: "I may be the last survivor of Canada's first national internment operations. What happened to our family, to many of our friends, can never be undone. It was unwarranted. It was unjust. But

March 29, 1993
Oral Questions
I believe that you, Mr. Prime Minister, have a unique and historic opportunity to show understanding and compassion for those who fell victim. Before you leave office I appeal to you to honour the Ukrainian Canadian community's request for acknowledgement and redress. Do what is right and just".
I urge the Prime Minister and his government to listen to these pleas and settle this issue.

Mr. Speaker, recently I sent questionnaires to my constituents to get their feedback on federal issues. Already thousands of surveys have been returned to my office. The high rate of response demonstrates my constituents' awareness of federal issues. They care about what goes on in Ottawa and they keep themselves informed.
When asked what federal issue is currently of greatest concern, one of the most common responses is the debt. Other issues of concern include the Young Offenders Act, the environment, and accountability of elected officials.
The overwhelming sense I am getting from these surveys is that the federal government must continue to reduce its spending. Edmontonians are prepared for the hard decisions that must be made, but they want their elected officials to share the burden. In particular my constituents think that the MP pension plan should be reviewed. They also feel that too much financial support is given to special interest groups.
Finally, the majority of respondents support the GST. They recognize that the GST is necessary but they insist that revenues continue to apply exclusively to debt reduction.
My constituents clearly want to be involved in the political process. We must make every effort to be responsive to their concerns.

Mr. Speaker, from March 28 to April 18 the Body Shop retail chain will be conducting a national campaign to
combat child poverty. Its 105 stores will be displaying giant posters declaring that child poverty is a national disgrace. Their staff will be initiating letter-writing campaigns and encouraging community schools and city officials to become more involved in alleviating child poverty. In short, they will be devoting money and time to help reduce child poverty in Canada.
All of this comes at a time when the federal government has been busy looking at ways to redefine poverty rather than to solve it.
In 1984 over four million Canadians were living in poverty in this country and more than one million of them were children. According to the most recent statistics, still more than four million Canadians live in poverty and still more than one million of them are children.
The Body Shop is to be congratulated for its efforts to broaden awareness of poverty issues in Canada and for taking concrete action where the present government has only provided rhetoric.
This government should listen very carefully to this socially conscious business and act now to alleviate child poverty.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister.
On the weekend two of his colleagues implied that the government and the party they may lead some day plan to cut social programs, especially medicare. On the other hand, on Friday the Minister of Finance, who was touring the country, announced that the government did not intend to drop the helicopter purchase program which to date will cost $5.8 billion.
I would like the Minister of Finance to tell me if he had a choice between cutting social programs and maintaining the $5.8 billion helicopter purchase which option he would choose, helicopters or maintaining social programs in Canada?
March 29, 1993

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been attempting to put in place the appropriate fiscal measures so that we can preserve and maintain the social safety net that we and Canadians have all been very proud of and wish to retain.
The difficulty we have is with the growing percentage of our revenues being allocated for debt servicing costs. It imposes very direct pressure upon our ability to finance social programs.
We have been attempting to take steps to stimulate growth, to encourage investment and to encourage job creation while at the same time contain expenditures and reduce the deficit as a percentage of GDP. That is what we have been doing and we have been quite successful in that regard.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
It is
apparent, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance has no intention of commenting on the choice that the government has to make and that he does not want to cancel the famous helicopter program.
On Friday the Liberal Party indicated that there is a very urgent need at this moment for the government to get involved in the conversion of the national defence industry. Commenting on that proposition the Minister of National Defence said that it was a very "poor excuse for policy" and full of "bogus terminology".
I would like to know from the Minister of Finance if it is the view of this government that making sure there is a smooth transition from the military industry to a peacekeeping type of industry is not the priority of this government. The Americans have been moving into that field for some time now.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. Leader of the Opposition is commenting on why the government is not following the American example.
One of the reasons of course is that 60 per cent of the U.S. industry in the general defence sector is actually on defence projects. In Canada 70 per cent of our defence
Oral Questions
industry sector actually is in civilian production, not military production.
The Liberal Party said the DIPP program should be diverted to civilian use. In fact 80 per cent of DIPP expenditures are now diverted to civilian use. The reality is the problem that he is addressing is not the same problem in Canada that it is in the United States.
This is an important industry. As long as we are going to have an Armed Forces, and we will require one for the foreseeable future, I think it is appropriate that Canadian industry be able to supply at least some of the equipment the forces need.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, is the minister aware that there was a subcommittee of this House that produced a report last October indicating the need to move in that field quickly? Five members of that committee were members of his own party. They presented a unanimous report to the House of Commons. Why is the government not listening to the House of Commons rather than just dismissing some very important problems in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Not at all. We take reports of committees of this House of Commons very seriously. An example is the unanimous report of the House to get rid of the MST and replace it with a GST.
Another example is the unanimous report of a committee of this House, including Liberals and the NDP, to go ahead with the EH-101 helicopter contract. In terms of the report the hon. member was talking about, we do concede that primarily as a result of the referendum campaign this was put aside in view of other priorities, but it is the intention of the government to table a response to this report very soon.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance.
In his financial statement last December the government made a number of major defence cuts which severely limited our capacity to provide full-time professional peacekeeping forces. As a result 50 per cent of our peacekeepers are now reservists who have had to have a rush training.

March 29, 1993
Oral Questions
Now the Minister of Finance says he refuses to cut helicopters but he is going to make other defence cuts, once again clearly endangering the capacity of this country to provide full, effective and efficient peacekeeping sources. In fact, we do not have a defence policy.
I ask the Minister of Finance if this government will table a new relevant defence policy before it brings forth a budget so that we will have a defence policy made for defence priorities and not simply by the Minister of Finance?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to begin with, as I understand the position of the Liberal Party the EH-101 should not be proceeded with and instead we should update the ancient Sea Kings and Labradors.
The EH-101 calls for an expenditure of $350 million a year for 13 years. Updating the Sea Kings and Labradors would require about the same annual expenditure each year for the next six or seven years, after which we would end up with 40-year old helicopters nowhere near the equivalent of the EH-lOls and unable to go out in really bad weather for search and rescue.
In terms of reservists the hon. member should take some time to meet some of our reservists because our reservists are first class, well trained and are not put into positions where they are in danger for lack of training. We have had a total force concept in place for a number of years and it is working rather well.

Mr. Speaker, it may come as information and I am sure it does to the hon. minister that in fact the United States marine corps and air force and the Japanese defence force are now flying updated Sea Kings with adequate and efficient capabilities to provide for search, rescue and anti-submarine warfare at one-tenth the cost of the EH-101 helicopters. It is about time this government began to understand the real priorities of this country.
I come back to the Minister of National Defence. Six months ago after extensive hearings the committee reported that there should be a major program of defence conversion. I want to quote from that committee: "The aim is to foster a leading edge, civilian as well as military, high technology in areas such as surveillance monitoring, verification, sovereignty protection and peacekeeping". That report was endorsed by Conservative members of the committee.
I ask the Deputy Prime Minister: Why did the Minister of National Defence speaking on behalf of the government reject this report in her statement on Friday? Why does this government not listen to a committee of the House of Commons including its own members?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there was no rejection of the report. As I indicated, the report has not been responded to yet by the government.
In terms of conversion, as I indicated in response to the hon. member's leader, the Liberal Party has not even identified the problem, let alone the solution.
When it comes to the question of whether government should decide what industries should be pursued, we happen to believe the private sector can make those decisions better than government. We do not think there is any evidence anywhere in the world to show that governments do a good job of selecting winners as opposed to the private sector.
The hon. member might define what peacekeeping technologies are other than spy satellites. We are already involved in the satellite business to a high degree. How much more does he want?
It's in the report, Harvie. Read the report.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The report has been read.
If the member is talking about environmental industries, he should check the record. He will see that the Canadian private sector is responding very vigorously to the opportunities in the environmental sector.
What the world has learned, but apparently not the hon. member, is that the private sector makes better decisions on priorities than governments.
March 29, 1993

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Today Statistics Canada published figures showing there is a real crisis in daycare in this country. More than half our children urgently need quality daycare. Parents can find none at an affordable price. Nevertheless this government remains adamant about not wanting to establish a national program that would provide quality, affordable day care and it remains intent on spending $5.8 billion on helicopters. Why not spend this money on our children? Do it, and do it now.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to listen to the hon. member one would draw the conclusion that the government is not spending any money on children and does not consider children as a priority.
For the record and for all hon. members, perhaps it is timely to put on the record the kind of support that the federal government is providing to support children. Income support programs for 1993 in the form of a child tax-
You cut it out in B.C. and Ontario.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, they ask the question and if they do not want the answer-
Thlk about child care.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: I will get to that. In terms of income support the child tax benefit provides $5.1 billion; social assistance, $1.5 billion; CPP child benefits, $280 million; GST credit, $750 million; the employment support program, UI maternity and parental care, $1.4 billion; child care expense deductions, $300 million; child care under the CAP training program, $400 million, for a grand total of $9.3 billion per year. That is the amount for this year.

Mr. Speaker, it is clear that this government backed down on its promise in 1984 and 1988 to bring in a national child care program. The only conclusion Canadians can make is that this government agrees with the Conservative MP for Fraser
Oral Questions
Valley West who said essentially: "I see day care centres as little more than temporary orphanages".
I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister if he is in agreement with that and if he feels that having over 600,000 children in unlicensed child care facilities is building a future for this country.
Will the Deputy Prime Minister build a real legacy for Canadian children and make sure that in the next budget his government brings in a national child care program?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Even the hon. member acknowledges the fact that we have a serious fiscal problem. It is encouraging to note that the leader in the province of Ontario is starting to recognize that fact.
Notwithstanding that, we have tried to appropriate a fair amount of money toward support of children, toward the support of maintaining the social safety net.
If the hon. member is suggesting that $9.3 billion which is directed to aid in support for children is an insignificant amount, then she and I are on different wavelengths.
While the hon. member suggests that she can spend $130 billion over the next five years and still bring the deficit down by $11 billion, I cannot follow her mathematics in that regard.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I cannot follow this government's logic.
This government says yes to cold war helicopters, yes to not taxing the wealthy's private trusts, yes to a business lunch deduction that costs Canadian taxpayers $1 billion but it says no to the children of Canada. By not putting in real programs it says no to making sure that Canadians get back to work.
Why give the rich a free lunch while there are children with no lunch? Will the Deputy Prime Minister look seriously at addressing the needs of children in this country and at the need for a national child care program so that their parents can participate in training, education and the work force?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government is not turning its back on children. It has improved the

March 29, 1993
Oral Questions
programs for children step by step. A $9.3 billion program in support of children is certainly not an insignificant amount.
In terms of creating opportunities for job creation and new economic activity and growth, the hon. member is criticizing the small business sector. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
Approximately 11 months ago, 26 miners lost their lives at the Westray coal mine. A provincial inquiry has been stalled. The Nova Scotia government has lost $12 million. The federal government has lost $80 million. The families of the deceased miners are without answers as to how this tragedy occurred.
In view of the importance of the subject matter I ask the Deputy Prime Minister if he has now sought a progress report on the investigation from the commissioner of the RCMP. If so, will he share that information with the House? If not, why not?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not at all sure that would be an appropriate thing for the government to do in terms of trying to direct the RCMP or to put pressure on it with regard to the matter. I am sure the RCMP will do its usual diligent job in that regard.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as usual the hon. minister opposite wishes to twist the question.
What we are seeking from the Government of Canada is to ascertain from the commissioner of the RCMP
where this investigation is going. Twenty-six men have lost their lives.
In point of fact, when we asked for information on the Westray disaster we received very little. The government would not tell us its role in the funding of this particular disaster. We had to go to the access to information provisions. We got 18 blank pages, 18 censored pages. That is what we received from the Government of Canada.
Will the minister responsible explain to Canadians why the government is covering up the information contained in those documents?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows the Access to Information Act contains restrictions on what can be released.
For example, personal private information cannot be released because of the protection of the Privacy Act. There is commercial information which again is covered by other pieces of legislation and we simply cannot release it.
However, as the hon. member should know, all of this information has been given to the commission of inquiry in the province of Nova Scotia. The government is pleased that the legal obstacles to that commission have been removed. The commission will now be able to perform its function with access to all of the available information.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the same minister on the same subject.
The minister knows that with respect to the Westray file $80 million of public funds have been lost by the federal government. Twelve million dollars of public funds have been lost by the Nova Scotia government. More important, 26 lives have been lost. Eighteen pages have not been lost; they have been hidden. They concern not personal information but public information about what cabinet knew, when it knew and what advice was made available.
Does the minister recognize a year later, a year after 26 lives were lost, that now is the time to come clean and give the people of Canada, and more important the

people of Pictou county, all the information with respect to this terrible and tragic mine disaster?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
As the hon. member knows, it was indeed a terrible disaster. This whole House was very sympathetic with the losses suffered by the families. The mine was proceeded with at the strong urging of everybody in Pictou county because of its economic benefits.
The disaster occurred. The mine is regulated by provincial jurisdiction, as the hon. member knows. The province has decided, I think quite properly, to proceed with an independent commission of inquiry. This government is co-operating 100 per cent with that commission of inquiry. It has provided all the information available to the commission of inquiry. I am sure the hon. member would not want to be accused of taking partisan advantage of a tragedy that has occurred and will let due process establish the truth.

Mr. Speaker, there are the 18 pages missing under access to information on the request for information on financing, on funding, on cabinet information, what information was in its hands when it made decisions about providing $80 million. Not only is that information missing, but specifically the CANMET report which was made public by the government last June and which we understood at the time was a complete document is missing seven additional pages, as we now see under the access to information request. Seven additional pages are missing in the CANMET report dealing with the suitability and advisability of proceeding with development of this mine and in fact, safety issues.
Given that it is not the provincial government and not the mine but the federal government that is burying or hiding 25 pages of crucial evidence about what cabinet knew and what advice was given to cabinet before $80 million of federal public funds were made available, does the minister not believe now, one year later, that it is appropriate that all evidence be laid on the table and that the cover-up end?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no matter how loud the hon. member may raise his voice, that does not permit the government to break the law in respect to access to information.
Oral Questions
The hon. member would be suitably and quite properly outraged if the government were to release his income tax files. Why does he not have the same concern for the privacy that might be violated through taking the kind of action he is suggesting we undertake?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment.
I would like to question the minister regarding the ever-shrinking green plan. I would like the minister to explain why he has never publicly challenged the cuts from the green plan which has shrunk from the original Bouchard promise of $6 billion over five years to $5 billion over five years, to $3 billion over five years, to $3 billion over six years, to a 36 per cent cumulative cut for the coming year.
Would the minister tell Canadians why he has accepted these kinds of cuts to Canada's fragile environment in silence?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot agree with the premise on which the member bases his question in terms of what had been said previously. One thing we have to establish is that the green plan itself, which is a sustainable development plan for Canada, is more than just the amount of money in the plan. Neither is it exclusively everything that we are doing in the area of the environment or sustainable development.
What we see in terms of expenditures over the last two years, for example, is that we have spent close to half a billion dollars in the area of sustainable development, specifically under the confines of the green plan. From year one to year two there has been a 36 per cent increase in spending.
If the hon. member wanted to look at the projected spending for the next year, he would also find there is a projected increase in spending of 23 per cent. That is a very substantial increase in spending in a period of fiscal restraint.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to hear the minister talking about sustainable development because I am sure he has now read with care the ruling of

March 29, 1993
Oral Questions
the trial division of the Federal Court in relation to the fixed link to Prince Edward Island.
Not just the people in P.E.I. or New Brunswick but I think Canadians generally would like to know the position of someone who aspires to be the leader of his party and is presently the Minister of the Environment and therefore responsible for environmental assessment. Will the minister rise in his place and say today publicly that at least he supports a full, proper, public environmental assessment of the bridge proposed between Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows very well that with regard to the environmental assessment process of the federal government which is now an Order in Council, we have had 54 court rulings over a period of time. The hon. member participated directly in the discussions. The government brought forward new legislation to deal with the issue of environmental assessment. In fact, we recently signed an agreement with Alberta for a one-window approach in this area.
That being said, we are actively discussing the ruling of the Federal Court in regard to the fixed link. We are going to have some discussions on how to approach it. There are legal considerations. There are two main points in the ruling: one relates to the environmental assessment itself and the other deals with a constitutional issue. We will want to examine those issues and come forward with a decision on how to proceed as rapidly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment.
No amount of creative accounting can disguise repeated cuts to the green plan. In December last year in the mini budget the Minister of Finance announced and the Minister of the Environment confirmed there would be $440 million this year in green plan spending. We now know that the government plans to spend only $351 million. That is another cut of 20 per cent, $90 million from the green plan.
Will the minister now confirm that the $90 million has gone out of the green plan and into a slush fund for pre-election spending?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, only my Liberal friend could in the same question accuse us of cutting and creating slush funds at the same time or simultaneously.
What I can answer and offer in terms of a response to my friend is a report we put out today, as we had committed to do, on the progress of the green plan itself. The numbers speak for themselves.
For the first year $210 million has been spent. For the year ending in a few days $286 million extra has been spent. That is close to half a billion dollars. If you project that in terms of its increase, it is a 36 per cent increase. If we look into the next year, we have an increase in funding of 23 per cent. That is the expenditures of Canadian taxpayers' money in the area of the green plan and sustainable development. I think it is a very, very substantial increase in spending.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
The figures do, indeed, speak for themselves. When the green plan was announced in December of 1990, the government promised $3 billion over five years, or $600 million a year. In the plan's first three years the government has met less than half of that commitment.
I refer to the C.D. Howe Institute report of 1991 where it predicted that: "The green fund is likely to be used as a war chest for the Progressive Conservative government's campaign plans".
I ask the minister, why is the green plan left dying on the vine to store up a pre-election spending binge by his government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the green plan, which is Canada's sustainable development plan, is recognized throughout the world as being one of the most innovative sustainable development plans that has been produced. There is good reason for that; it is in our interest to do that. Given the fact that our economy is based on natural resources, we are one of the industrialized countries in the world that lives the most off our environment.
In the area of the environment over all, the government is recognized as having done a lot. That is what President Clinton was able to recognize. I am sorry that
March 29, 1993

my hon. friend cannot do that. Just in the last year we dealt with the issue of CFCs and climate change. New regulations came forward in the area of the pulp and paper industry. We also brought forward new legislation, Bill C-42, the Wild Animal and Plant Protection Act. Bill C-13 came forward in the last year. We increased surveillance over the last year 40 per cent from where it was the year before.
We attended the earth summit in Rio de Janeiro. My hon. friend was there with us. We signed and ratified two international conventions, one on climate change, one on biodiversity, the first country in the world to do that.
I know you are very interested in this, Mr. Speaker, and I am glad you are asking me to go on. All of this was done by the government in the last year throughout the-
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of the Environment, whom I wish well in his bid for the leadership of his party.
There is a widening gap between the government's preaching abilities and its actions. Both at home and abroad there has been a litany of broken promises.
Why has the government broken its commitment made in Rio by cutting and suspending aid to the poorest of the poor nations of this world? Why is the government so reluctant in refusing to ratify the Law of the Sea Convention? Why has the government missed the deadline for assessing 33 persistent toxic chemicals listed in the Canadian Environmental Protection Act? Why is the government failing to produce a national strategy for stabilizing greenhouse emissions? Why-
That is certainly a collective question. I hope that the minister will be able to answer it expeditiously.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me address a few of those issues.
As far as toxic substances are concerned we have a priority substance list that includes 44 substances. An agreement was reached after an extensive stakeholder
Oral Questions
period dealing with that. We have dealt with 20 of those substances. We published reports on six.
In the area of climate change we have signed an international convention and ratified it December last. We have also made a commitment to producing by next spring our national report on climate change. We are working on an economic instruments paper concerning tradable permits to be able to put forward the solutions and the tools we need in the area of climate change. We have maintained our commitment to stabilization of 1990 levels.
I think we will try another question.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps the minister may want to answer the following supplementary question.
Why does the finance department review the environmental regulations from a competitive perspective? Why is the government of which he is a member not allowing the environment department to conduct a review from a sustainability perspective as well?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think my friend is referring to a process by which different departments were reviewing the regulations from a competitiveness perspective.
I want to stress that in our department we have worked a lot on the regulatory process. There is a recognition that we have to regulate better. Among the things we have to do for example is complement our regulatory approach with a voluntary approach and also through economic instruments.
We do have a stakeholder process assisting us to develop regulations so that they are presented in the most sustainable way possible for our economy.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister of immigration. It concerns procedures for applying the new guidelines for women refugee claimants who face gender discrimination.
The minister is aware that 35 women who fear persecution as a result of their gender are to be deported because they arrived in Canada before the new immigra-

March 29, 1993
Oral Questions
tion rules took effect. Will the minister declare a moratorium on the deportation of these women and their children and allow them to remain in Canada on humanitarian and compassionate grounds?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when we review a case all factors are taken into account. That includes the principles behind the guidelines on gender persecution which were issued on March 9, as well as any new information which is available concerning a rejected claimant's current situation and the situation in his or her home country. This is the process that takes place and it ensures fairness to all rejected refugee claimants.

Mr. Speaker, I would hope that the minister, instead of just rubber stamping the previous opinions of local officials, which is what happened last week, would re-evaluate cases according to these new guidelines.
For Canada to deport women back to countries where they and their children face discrimination, depravation and danger is both cruel and inhumane. Why will the minister not use his ministerial powers and discretion to allow women like Amina Mohamed and these 34 other women who face gender discrimination to remain in Canada on humanitarian and compassionate grounds? Why will he not do this?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, between myself and my office literally hundreds of immigration cases are reviewed on humanitarian and compassionate grounds each year.
Some of them are accepted and some are refused. I have no intention of listing those cases. For this fiscal year, the policies and decisions of the government have resulted in more than 73,000 cases being approved on humanitarian and compassionate grounds alone.
That is almost equal to the total number of immigrants that the Liberal Party of Canada let into Canada in 1984.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister of fisheries. It refers to the lobster fishermen in the Northumberland Strait.
For more than two years the lobster fishermen in the Northumberland Strait have voluntarily accepted a larger carapace size for lobsters. During that time they have asked the DFO to also accept that larger carapace size in regulation.
Last week DFO announced that it would not accept the larger carapace size. Would the department reconsider its decision and if not, why not?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question of lobster carapace size is one of divided opinion in the maritime provinces, particularly between certain lobster fishermen located in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia as compared to lobster fishermen in Prince Edward Island.
About one year ago, with the agreement of the three provincial governments involved, we appointed a firm of consultants to do an in-depth study of the situation, whether this is a step that should be taken. We have the report of that study now but we have not had sufficient time to consult with all interested groups before the season opens on April 30.
While over all the report recommends that we should allow an increase in the carapace size-
Time.

speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: This is an important issue before anybody in the Liberal Party bellows time. Although the report points out that there are positive advantages to proceeding in this way, there would be a short-term decrease in employment in processing.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance and it deals with the annual minimum disbursement quota of registered foundations where they have to spend 4.5 per cent of their assets.
As everybody knows, for the last two years interest rates have been very quickly dropping, to the point where the income of these charitable foundations is very low. They do not have the resources they normally would have.
March 29, 1993

Is the minister planning on making changes in the way the government directs these foundations to disburse their assets?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is correct in what he says, the allocation of 4.5 per cent of the value of the assets of charitable organizations are to be devoted to charitable purposes.
I should tell the hon. member that there is no direct relationship between this formula and interest rates. In other words, this formula does not track interest rates. I will take the hon. member's submission as a representation but I am not contemplating any changes at this time.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the minister of health, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
Last week aboriginal leaders met in Ottawa at a National Suicide Prevention Workshop to discuss the growing crisis of youth suicides in their communities. Tragically at the same time two youths in one of the communities that I represent committed suicide within a day of each other.
The minister of health heard that the communities need both human and financial resources to design and implement their own crisis intervention programs.
We have been talking in this House, at least myself and many others, since 1988 about the crisis of youth suicide in aboriginal communities. I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister if it is time for action or is it still time to talk and talk and study the issue some more?

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to offer our deepest sympathies to the families of the two youths who took their lives last week in northern Ontario.
This cannot be resolved just by governments. There is a major problem with suicides specifically in our aboriginal communities. We are working with the aboriginal communities, the people and the band leaders to resolve some of their difficulties.
Oral Questions
However, all we have to do is just look back at the last few decades where most of the programs have been government-driven and have not succeeded. We have to work with the families and the band leaders to put in the necessary social services to give those youngsters some hope for the future.

I must say, with all due respect, Mr. Speaker, I have stood in this place many times and asked the same question and I continue to get the same answer, that we cannot just throw money at the issue and we have to let the communities do it themselves. The communities are still waiting for the government to make up its mind whether the issue of teen suicide, of mental health for aboriginal people, is truly a priority of the government.
If this were truly a priority of the government it would have already made up its mind to put this issue to the communities in order for them to create their own crisis intervention program.
I ask the member one last time before we go to the polls: Are we going to talk about it and talk about it or are we truly going to do something about this major crisis?

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will see that this is at the top of our agenda. We take it very seriously.
As I said before, we will offer social services for mental health and suicide treatment which is what the community wants and what the band leaders want. We will not act unilaterally, as has happened in the past, and see this fail. We are going to succeed. The only way we can succeed is through teamwork. That means the youngsters, the families, the bands, the governments, the communities and all the agencies working together to give those people hope.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Agriculture.
The U.S. market takes about 40 per cent of all beef produced in Canada and about 95 per cent of our beef exports. The Canadian Cattlemen's Association is now very worried that the Price Stabilization Program put in place by the government since 1985 is going to endanger these exports severely.

Privilege
Will the government tell us if it is prepared to accommodate our beef producers by changing the nature of this program?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Justice, Attorney General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, the National Tripartite Stabilization Program, which has been in place for several years, meets national standards for bilateral trade with the Americans as well as international trade standards. The U.S. government appeared three times before a binational panel on free trade but its claims were rejected. The program meets international regulations.
However, the Stabilization Program is now being reviewed by the parties involved. The provinces are also involved in the program. It is a tripartite program involving the provinces, the federal government and producers.
We are all working together to find ways to improve the program. We have never rejected it. However, any changes should not be considered in the light of problems we have with the Americans because there is absolutely no connection. We have stood firm so far. The program legally conforms to international regulations. We were successful in our claims before international tribunals, and this will happen again.

Mr. Speaker, that is not an answer to my question.

The minister knows that the Dunkel proposals at the ongoing GATT negotiations call for an end to price-based support for farm products.
Can our beef producers across Canada be assured that their proposals which are compatible with Mr. Dunkel's will be accepted and put into place this year?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Justice, Attorney General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had meetings with the Minister of
Finance and the Minister of Agriculture. We are meeting on a very regular basis. The Liberal Prime Minister at the time never met farm producers during the 16 years he was in power, but we are having meetings on an almost monthly basis now. We do not need any advice on how we should deal with these representatives.
We have introduced two national programs, NISA and GRIP, which are an adequate response to existing needs. We have the stabilization program, in place and these programs are being reviewed regularly. If we can make any improvements in response to current needs we will do so. We will not act unilaterally but in consultation with producers.

March 29, 1993

The petitioners state that the present social climate is such that many women feel intimidated or afraid to report incidents of assault or abuse, that aboriginal, visible minority, immigrant, disabled, lesbian and poor women face additional overwhelming barriers in reporting violence or abuse and receiving help.
Therefore, the undersigned, your petitioners, humbly pray and call upon Parliament to accept legislation designed to eliminate violence against women and children and to encourage and support women to report incidents of assault or abuse and to provide assistance and support for women reporting assault or abuse.
