speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in the debate this afternoon.
I had quite a bit of time to consider the remarks that I am about to make. Upon lengthy reflection, I want to address a few points. In particular, I want to support my colleague's Motion No. 1, concerning the infamous 21-year rule.
I want to offer my sincere thanks to the member for Sudbury who I know has been very active in condemning this issue as have several other members. The 21-year rule is the Robin Hood in reverse rule. It is designed specifically to give help to those who least need it, which sounds like government policy right away.
As my distinguished colleague from Algoma says, we all remember the GST, which is another example of laws designed to benefit the rich. Let us get into this 21-year rule. What will it do?
Professor Neil Brooks addressed the committee. He is associate dean of the Osgoode Law School. He said that this rule would provide an extension on private trusts that will clearly result in a number of Canada's wealthiest families paying less tax this year than they otherwise would. Let us get all of this straight. What are we doing here?
Many clauses in the bill are good. Some clauses are totally offensive, namely this one, which gives a tax break to the absolutely wealthiest people in Canada. Why does one want to give an additional tax break to billionaires?
I do not know about you, but I do not even know a billionaire. Why do we want to give them this kind of a tax break? I am looking forward to the 10-minute
Government Orders
speeches that we are having now on report stage for a government member to stand in this House and tell us why this is good for Canada.
Let us have none of this nonsense of saying this is a bill designed to help children or something like that. This is a bill designed to help the wealthy get a tax break at the expense of those at the other end who have been subjected to no less than 37 or 38 tax increases.
Thirty-eight now.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
My colleague from Algoma says 38 now, and he is always correct on this. We have been subjected to 38 different tax increases by the Conservative Party.
How does it work? It works roughly like this: Canada's wealthiest families will be able to defer paying taxes on the accrued capital gains, substantially what is beyond any other tax avoidance technique. In other words, once they have run out of all this other tax avoidance stuff they can invoke this particular rule. It is kind of like having two goalies in the net. In case the puck misses the first one the rich have this extra large hockey stick which can deflect anything right at the back of the first one. This would allow people to defer the paying of tax on capital gains. This has been described in the industry as estate freezing.
Not one reason for having this bill thus far invoked by the government even addresses, at least not in a substantial way, why it wants to have this clause in the bill or why it is necessary for us to retain it.
This is simply bad policy. It is bad policy because it tells Canadians at the lower end and medium end, and even some at the upper end, of the tax scale that there are ways around taxes providing people can establish these trusts and they are rich enough to know how to make them work.
There are other issues in this bill. One which I want to address very briefly is the capital gains exemption. I happen to be a person who thinks that there should not be capital gains exemptions, period. Even if the government and I disagree on that point the least we could agree on is that the rule be applied consistently to everyone. If the government is going to have the capital gains exemption rule, so be it. However, why does it exempt particular kinds of assets the way it has?
Let me give a parallel. If one plays the stock market on speculative stock on the Vancouver Stock Exchange, for

March 29, 1993
Government Orders
instance, penny stocks and the like, that is capital gains exempt. Any accrual of capital gains is exempt from tax, up to the maximum of $100,000 providing it qualified. On the other hand, a small investor at home who buys the apartment block next door, or who wants to build an apartment building with three units in it-not one with a bunch of employees that can be written off as a business but just one building next door to that person's house, and we do have a housing shortage in Canada right now-later on when that person sells the triplex then that person would pay capital gains on that.
This is at the same time as we have exempted the investor that I just described a few moments ago and we have exempted someone selling his horse in Kentucky or his painting somewhere in a gallery, perhaps not even in Canada. The accrual of capital gains on the horse or painting I have just described would be tax exempt, but selling the vacant lot or selling the triplex apartment building next door would not be exempt. Why? Why are we doing this to people involved in that particular industry?
Personally I do not own any kind of real estate other than my own home. My constituents are complaining about this. Yes, people in the real estate business are complaining as well, and I have good reason to hear what real estate agents say, with two of them in my own household. However, this is not designed to benefit real estate agents but to plug up a perceived loophole for investors in real estate, not for people who sell it.
Those investors in small real estate units no longer can have this deduction. I and my colleagues say: Have one rule and have it for everyone. If the government wants to do away with the exemption, there was none when this government came to power in 1984 so I cannot criticize that. However, it should not pick selectively as it is doing now because that is wrong.
My colleagues have made all these points in our representation at the committee level. We have introduced amendments and we feel that they are important. Many measures in this bill are good measures but those two, the ones I have just described, are not. In particular, the frozen trust issue or the 21-year rule is bad. It is simply bad and we should not renew those provisions at all. We are clearly sending a bad message to the people
of Canada, particularly at a time of record debt and record deficit, mostly caused by this government across the way. We are sending a message to Canadians that we want to tax the poor more and tax the rich less. That is the long and the short of it and I want no part of it.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to stand today and speak in support of the amendment of the member for Sudbury with respect to clause 42 and the provisions of the private family trust legislation, bringing the family trust to a close and making family trusts taxable at the present time.
Let us start by looking at what a private family trust is. It is a legal instrument used to pass on assets to beneficiaries of the trust, who are often spouses, children or grandchildren. Even a simple private trust costs thousands of dollars to set up, so it is apparent from this definition that private family trusts are set up by those who are eminently wealthy, those with lots of money behind them who are specifically looking for loopholes and ways to legally avoid taxation.
Let us look at the history of this legislation. The current legislation, which is presently drawing to a close, covering the private family trusts goes back 21 years to 1972 during the Liberal administration when it eliminated the estate taxes and the capital gains tax was introduced. This provision then exempted from being taxed for the period of 21 years assets put into a family trust, the idea being that they could escape paying taxes on the assets held within the trust itself for that period of time until maturity of 21 years when taxation would be paid on the capital assets of the trust itself.
What the proposal in this legislation does is extend that exemption from 21 years to the lifetime of the person for whom it is held in trust. The arguments by the government side for doing this are varied and many.
One of the arguments used is that this will help those people who are disabled and that it would be unfair to tax them now. To contradict that particular argument it is very clear that over a 21-year period of time there is a lot of time to have set up the alternatives to paying lump sum taxation. There are provisions within the Income Tax Act allowing the income tax to be paid over a 10-year period.
March 29, 1993

It is fairly clear that if people have 21 years, which is more time than most of us have for various tax provisions, to set up and get ready for a tax it is only reasonable to think that after that period of time provision would have been made within the trust to pay it out. It seems that this change is simply a method of once again rewarding the wealthy and the supporters of the government.
Let us look at some things that some professionals are saying about these particular changes. I would like to quote three of the professionals who have appeared before the committee or who have had things to say about this. The first one is Sidney Goldstein, of Goldstein & Goldstein in Ottawa, who said simply:
There is no question that it represents a massive windfall for existing trusts.
Kathryn Bush of Blake Cassels said:
A cynical person might suggest that pressure from influential political supporters also should be listed as a reason for the draft legislation.
Neil Brooks, the associate dean of Osgoode Hall Law School, said:
The government has given Canada's wealthiest families notice that it intends to give them a gift worth several billion dollars.
Let us look at some of the evidence that was given before the legislative committee on Bill C-92. I refer specifically to the evidence given by Mr. Sidney Goldstein, who said in his introductory remarks:
- given the view that there was some affiliation with Tbries,
Referring to himself he said:
I too am questioning the appropriateness and purposes of this proposal.
He then went on to state further in his evidence:
The proposal here, and I second Professor Brooks' comment, is more generous than any other proposal in the act.
He was referring to the Income Thx Act. He continued:
One of the propositions that was raised here in this committee was that it was really no different from deferring tax by giving everything to your children. Here you're just deferring tax until the last of your children dies, or that's the theory.
The fact is that's not what's being done. The deferral is until the last of a class of persons dies, potentially.
He went on to state:
Government Orders
- the potential tax benefits from this proposal are in the millions of dollars.
Toward the end of his testimony he stated as follows:
There is no suggestion here that any particular use of these funds for any particular benefit is going to be encouraged as a result of this proposal.
It is clear that this is a tax windfall to these people. There is a cost to the federal government, to our revenue coffers, that amounts to a substantial amount of money.
It is not unlike the arguments of the Ministry of Finance when it is asked about the tax havens and the tax loopholes uncovered by the Auditor General of Canada, which we in our party have been pointing out for a long time. The government simply says that to be competitive we must allow them to exist. Yet when we talk to the officials from Revenue Canada they tell us that there are many ways of closing those tax loopholes. They say there are many things that can be done that will not impede the competitiveness of our international corporations but will make billions of dollars.
It has been suggested to me by one Revenue Canada tax official that billions of dollars in taxes are flowing out of this country as a result of these tax havens. This is simply another example of the government refusing to bring in fair taxation, of the government refusing to attack the wealthiest in this nation to ensure they pay their fair share.
Let me turn just briefly to the comments of Dr. Neil Brooks, associate dean of Osgoode Hall. He said that the amendment in this particular bill, Bill C-92:
-will clearly result in a number of Canada's wealthy families paying less tax this year than they otherwise would. There just can't be any question about that.
In Dr. Brooks' final comment to the committee he stated that the amendment:
-is bad tax policy because there is absolutely no theoretical tax justification for the amendment that's being proposed. It will only benefit high-income people.
That is why I must support the member for Sudbury in her amendment to ensure that the trust provisions that were brought in have a termination point which is the same as when it was set up back in 1972. The time to end that is January 1, 1993. It should be ended. This particular provision should not be allowed to go through to give the wealthiest families in Canada that further tax break. They have had 21 years to prepare for their taxation.

Now I say to those wealthy families in Canada: "Pay the piper. The time has come to help Canada and the rest of Canadians get a fair taxation system on the ground now".

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to add my comments to this debate today after having been a part of the debate for about three years actually through consultation with the Department of Transport, officials and various ministers.
I have taken an interest in this bill because I have a little history in the transportation business having been an auto retailer for almost 20 years and a manufacturer of travel trailers and other kinds of trailers. I have been very much involved with the Motor Vehicle Safety Act in both the retail and manufacturing areas.
For about three years we have had exhaustive discussions with the industry, consumers affairs organizations and organizations representing all aspects of the automobile industry. I do believe that we have as a group exhausted all possible permutations and combinations of possibilities for this bill. There have been many people and organizations involved with this and I was just one of them.
I had a chance to express my views here in the House on several occasions. I think it was nine altogether. I testified at a Senate committee on the bill. I have spoken to three separate ministers of transport on the bill and I spent virtually endless hours with officials explaining my position and my concerns with the bill.
Basically my concerns were that there was a double standard. It resulted from U.S. cars being allowed to be imported into Canada and qualified under a separate standard than cars brought through the Canadian system. There were two sets of rules. One was for imported cars and the other was for non-imported cars. That had a serious effect on consumers and their safety. It also had an impact on the business community where there was a double standard and not a level playing field.
To make a three-year story a little shorter, I would just like to say that through the good work of the committee in amendments and discussion they have come through with some amendments that address all my concerns and resolve them all. They create an opportunity to develop further regulations to implement the principles as outlined in the amendments to the bill. Generally speaking I come away very satisfied with the system. It works. All the organizations that expressed their concerns about the bill have been heard from and certainly there has been a consensus on the result. I think it will satisfy most of the participants.
I personally would like to express my own appreciation to the Department of Transport officials who have spent virtually endless hours with me on this. They have had a great deal of patience and a great deal of understanding in trying to see my point of view, which I did my best to express. I eventually was successful in explaining to them my concerns in such a way that they were able to agree to
March 29, 1993

the amendments that would correct any problem I had with Bill S-8.
The officials have taken a great deal of time to understand my position and also the positions of all the organizations both from the business community and the consumers groups that have expressed themselves.
They have asked me actually to thank the organizations, associations and officials that have taken a lot of time to develop briefs and to make presentations both to them individually, to them as Department of Transport officials and also to the committee. They appreciate the input and the briefs from all aspects. I too appreciate the industry and the associations that have taken a lot of time and trouble to develop these proposals and briefs.
With the amendments to the bill certainly there will be a lot more input required and a lot more co-operation from consumers, consumers' associations and the industry to make sure the principles outlined in the bill and the amendments are implemented in the best possible way with the least possible paper work. This is so that they will affect the industry and consumers in a positive way and in reflection of the principles outlined.
I and the department officials and the Minister of Transport all look forward to that continuing co-operation with the associations. We are most anxious to get on with it when the bill passes and receives Royal Assent.
I would again like to thank the officials for their patience in dealing with me over the years with this issue and I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity to speak my piece on the bill.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on behalf of the national Liberal caucus on this bill.
I want to congratulate the hon. member for Ottawa South who is the Liberal transport critic as you will know, Mr. Speaker, and as I am sure as all Canadians know. I congratulate him for his fine work and other
Government Orders
Liberal colleagues both in this House and in the other place who have worked toward this bill.
I want to indicate first of all our support for the current piece of legislation. I recognize there is a need to have rules with regard to the importation of vehicles that will be beneficial to Canadians, will not harm trade and certainly not cause major inconveniences for Canadians.
We know that at the present time, particularly since January 1, 1993, it is possible to import from the United States, at least theoretically, any car no matter how new. Prior to the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement cars that were less than 15 years old were effectively barred from entry into Canada. Cars that were older than 15 years were designated as antiques, I think. They were permitted to be purchased providing the duties and so on were paid.
With the advent over recent years of rules with regard to motor vehicle safety such as emissions and so on, it became clear that the newer cars being imported could still have other problems at the border even if they were allowed into Canada under the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. There is the situation where for instance many U.S. cars do not have metric odometers although some of them do. They have different rules on child restraint devices. It became difficult for people who were importing the vehicle to ascertain whether or not the vehicle they had already purchased could even be made to conform to these new rules.
Now with the national safety mark and with the passage of Bill S-8 there will be a framework at least by which this will be made possible.
Of course we are still concerned with ensuring that cars that come into this country whether new or used-I say that on behalf of my colleagues-are as green as possible. I am not referring to the colour of the dashboard or the paint job but to the requirement for emission standards to be such that they ensure that cars will provide for the cleanest environment.
There is also a section of this bill which provides for what is known as an emission credit where companies can actually bank on the fact that they have produced a large number of efficient cars and then they can trade in

March 29, 1993
Government Orders
some of these credits for a few gas guzzlers every now and then.
That is not such a bad thing in a way providing that these rules are progressively tightened. This is so that even if one does sell a gas guzzler, the over-all incentive is to produce more and more environmentally friendly vehicles. The idea is acceptable as long as that remains part of the understanding. It must remain not only the over-all objective but it has to be paramount in what is permitted in the legislation.
As one who has sat on the consumer and corporate affairs committee and the government operations committee of the House, I have long been concerned with the actions of some people in Canada whereby the new price stickers are removed seemingly by the retailer or perhaps by middlemen-or middle people if we cannot say that anymore in order to be politically correct-from the vehicles prior to arriving on the lot.
The difficulty with that is that the consumer is given the so-called retail price by people in the industry. He or she has no way to ascertain whether that information is authentic or whether one is getting an alleged $2,000 while the real discount is only about $10 or something.
It is very hard to get that information here in Canada. Increasingly we find cars on lots-I have had the experience many times-where someone very neatly with a razor blade removed all the amounts but not the motor vehicle description.
At the consumer and corporate affairs committee a couple of years ago I had occasion to question an automobile manufacturer who was there. I asked this manufacturer why it is that dealers do this in Canada. In the United States it is an offence to tamper with those stickers prior to the automobile being purchased by a customer.
He said: "Well, they were probably just cleaning the windows''. I said: "Is it not ironic that people clean windows in a strip about one and a half inches wide just where the numbers are and do not clean the rest of the window or the part of the sticker that has the description
of what the car has except for that part which has the amount?"
That was just a little hard to believe. I even suggested to that witness at that time that he should speak at a committee as though he were under oath, not putting too fine a point on it. In other words, I did not believe him.
I want to bring that to the attention of the House. As the automobile industry becomes more and more of a trans-border one-like it or not, that is done-I think it is important for us to ensure that at the very least the consumers on this side of the border get the same kind of protection that the consumers are getting on the other side. This is particularly so when as soon as a car is one day old one can sell it across the border with relative ease at the present time.
It is important that our consumers be given every benefit that consumers are getting south of the border as well. I thought it was a good occasion to bring this issue to the attention of the House. Perhaps there is an off chance that automobile manufacturers are listening to the debate this afternoon. I hope that when they clean windows in the future they do not clean them in strips one and a half inches wide where the numbers are and leave the rest of it there.
In future all the people interested can have a look at what was the manufacturer's suggested retail price. Then they can compare that with the alleged discount that any dealer says he or she is giving on the car. They can find out whether or not the so-called deal or savings they are getting is the one that is being announced by the dealer as such.
With that I will conclude my remarks and again add my words of appreciation to the hon. member for Ottawa South and other colleagues for their fine work at the committee stage and at earlier stages of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in third reading debate of Bill S-8, the Motor Vehicle Safety Act.
I am a member of the Standing Committee on Transport which reviewed this legislation. We took the bill out of this House and sent it to committee. We thought perhaps one or two witnesses might deal with the specific elements contained within the bill, such as the new rules regarding imported automobiles, the emission credits or
March 29, 1993

the consolidation of the legislation. What surprised me was the number of people who came in to talk about the question of wrecked vehicles being brought across the border and the interprovincial trade of wrecked vehicles. That followed a concern I had raised during debate at second reading, which in turn was prompted by some work the Thunder Bay Automotive Trades Association did in terms of making me aware of the issue.
I want to spend my time today talking about that aspect of the legislation. I think we saw a real willingness by the government and the departmental staff to work with the committee to find the appropriate way to deal with the concerns within the context of federal law. Obviously there are certain matters that are beyond the purview of the federal government. Once a vehicle has been manufactured and sold for the first time at the retail level it becomes the responsibility of the provincial authorities. One of the dilemmas we faced was how to do something in federal legislation that we genuinely wanted to do but found there were some very real barriers to doing.
I think the regulations prescribed by this bill will ensure that used vehicles coming across the border will be brought up to the appropriate safety standards. That is clear in the bill. They will also ensure they are also brought up to standard structurally.
The committee amended the bill. There was some wondering ahead of time whether a bill that started out in the other place would be easily amended in the House of Commons, knowing full well that once it was amended it would have to go back to the other place. But to the credit of the government members on the committee that was not an obstacle. In fact the amendment I am going to read was put forward by them in response to a number of issues that had been raised by me and witnesses before the committee. The amendment provides for some greater flexibility, but also greater certainty with the regulations. I just want to read it into the record.
The bill was to be amended by striking out lines 21 to 33 on page 5 and substituting the following therefor:
(2) except as otherwise provided by the regulations, a vehicle that has been sold at the retail level in the United States and that fails to
Government Orders
satisfy an applicable requirement of section 5 or 6 may be imported into Canada, notwithstanding that section, if the person importing the vehicle makes a declaration in the prescribed form and manner that before the vehicle is presented for registration under the laws of the province the vehicle (a) will be made to conform to that requirement; and (b) will be certified in the prescribed form and manner to so conform by such person as may be designated by the regulations.
The second part of the amendment was that after line 44 on page 5 the following is added:
(4) a vehicle that is imported into Canada must conform to the standard prescribed for the class of equivalent non-imported vehicle or made to conform to the standard prior to the presentation for registration under the laws of a province.
It sounds complicated but the committee decided- and these amendments were supported by all members in the committee-to make it clear there has to be a process. People cannot just bring cars to the Canada-U.S. border and promise to repair them. The government cannot just hope they do. The government has recognized there needs to be some degree of certainty there.
As members will know, we normally do not see regulations when we are dealing with legislation. One of the problems we have from time to time is ensuring the regulations are actually going to do what they are supposed to do. We have a commitment from the officials of the department that before the regulations are finalized with regard to the question of automobile imports they will come back to us in the transport committee and ask for our reaction.
They have gone even further than that. They have already given us a broad outline of the kinds of things they want to do which will go a long way toward meeting a lot of the testimony we heard from the witnesses.
I just want to report to the House on those specifics.
Safety and emissions regulations governing importation are under the Motor Vehicle Safety Act administered by Transport Canada.
Transport Canada will establish a network of registered certifiers operating under the supervision of a national registrar. The system could be linked to existing manufacturers or dealer networks established indepen-

March 29, 1993
Government Orders
dently under a third party contracted to Transport Canada or be a combination of these options.
Just as an aside, one of the concerns we raised was about the person who lives in Red Lake who wants to bring in a vehicle. Does he or she have to come back to Thunder Bay, Dryden or Kenora where there is an authorized dealer, or can he or she have that work done in Red Lake and certified by a licensed authority or designated authority in that community? That is one of the things we are going to be looking at when the regulations come back to us.
A list is published quarterly of U.S. vehicles eligible for importation. Most vehicles will be included. Exceptions will be those U.S. vehicles not meeting Canadian occupant restraint standards and specialty vehicles such as limousines or recreational vehicles where compliance with U.S. or Canadian standards is unsubstantiated.
Canadian entry will require (a) proof of compliance with U.S. safety standards, either by statement of compliance label or letter from original manufacturer; (b) eligibility for importation based on compliance with specified standards, for example occupant restraint systems; (c) completion of Transport Canada documentation requirements including a vehicle description and an affidavit to bring the vehicle into compliance with required Canadian standards.
In addition, one of the items raised because of the testimony before the committee was the little known fact that any Canadian wanting to import a vehicle from the United States must give the U.S. authorities 72 hours notice of his or her intention to do so. We are told that very few, if any, people actually do that. Currently when somebody brings that car to the Canadian border-we all know one does not stop first at American Customs and then cross the river and check in at Canadian Customs, one just starts at the Canadian side-we do not ask about that.
We have asked the departmental officials to take a look at that specific item to see if we can require importers to show proof they have complied with American laws. That is one way to deal with the question of thefts. That is one way to deal with the question of vehicles that have been written off because a number of states can provide a description of the history of that
vehicle. That would assist the Canadian authorities in determining the appropriateness of that vehicle coming across or, at the very least, the degree of work required to bring that vehicle up to Canadian standards.
Getting back to the draft provisional list of possible regulations or the broad concepts, vehicle modifications are performed or may be performed by the importers' choice of company or by registered certifier. Notices of defect may be handled at no charge by a Canadian representative of the manufacturer or by the national registrar for a fee.
Vehicle modifications are inspected and approved by a registered certifier and documentation sent to the national registrar.
An approved copy of the documentation is provided to the importer for the proof of compliance necessary to have the vehicle licensed by a province.
One of the other areas we raised in committee is the question of vehicles that have been structurally damaged. We are hoping the regulations will be some kind of trigger mechanism that will require a licensed mechanic to at the very least take a look under the vehicle to see whether anything has been welded into the vehicle that should not be in a particular place, or whether there have been any welds to the frame. I want to come back to that in a moment.
That is the general direction the department is going to take in terms of the regulations. It has indicated it believes it can be back to us within approximately a month to run through the actual wording to see whether or not we feel it is suitable as it relates to what we have heard.
I want to turn to the question of wrecks. I do so in the context that in part this legislation does allow the federal government to take a look at those things coming across the Canada-U.S. border. Under Canadian constitutional law it really is difficult for us to deal with anything domestically. We know from testimony before the committee by the department officials that a committee of the Canadian Council of Motor Transport Administrators is attempting to develop a protocol nation-wide so that when a wrecked vehicle comes across this information is recorded and distributed to all provinces so they are aware of it. That is the second part of it.
March 29, 1993

There is a national committee made up of representatives of each of the provincial jurisdictions as well as the federal jurisdiction which is trying to come to grips with this.
Looking at some of the testimony presented to us in written form, this group was unable to appear. It is the Automotive Retailers Association of British Columbia. Its document was endorsed by the National Automotive Trades Association of Canada. The association which is an affiliation of regional and provincial associations representing Canada's retail automotive service industry in part says: "Our provincial affiliate in British Columbia has forwarded to you a brief which is representative of all of our member associations across Canada. We therefore wish to make you aware that NATA gives full endorsement to the brief submitted by ARA, the Automotive Retailers Association of British Columbia. It speaks on behalf of all of us".
I would like to read the section that deals with what is called rebuilt write-offs. It is entitled "The Nature of the Problem".
Insurance companies classify collision damaged vehicles as "write-offs" when the estimated cost of repairs exceeds the remaining actual cash value of the vehicle, or is greater than the cash value less the salvage value. The term "write-off", therefore, does not necessarily denote an inoperable wreck-nor a piece of junk! Frequently, it refers to a good, late model, low mileage vehicle which has suffered extensive collision damage that an insurer estimates would be uneconomical to repair. If properly rebuilt, such vehicles can provide adequate transportation and good value.
Insurance companies sell write-offs to the following classes of customers:
a)	Licensed auto recyclers or wreckers and used parts suppliers, who dismantle cars and sell undamaged used parts to body shops and other businesses, as well as to private customers.
b)	Licensed auto body shops and professional rebuilders.
And this is the key one:
c)	Private individuals-often amateur rebuilders.
The vehicles sold to body shops and rebuilders are repaired and returned, in most cases, to our roads and highways. Many of these units are rebuilt by qualified technicians using proper repair equipment techniques. As such, these vehicles once again may become an economical and safe mode of transportation.
Government Orders
However, many other rebuilt write-offs are rebuilt in dangerously unsafe fashion-either for private use or resale, by private individuals or amateur mechanics-who may be unskilled and ignorant and use inadequate tools and equipment. In such cases, frames may be spliced in unsafe places, such as beneath doors or in torsion boxes, which means welds result in rigidity in areas where manufacturers and designers intended a degree of "give" or yield. Also, steering and suspension parts, rods and spindles which arebent and which should be replaced are instead heated and hammered back into shape. The result is crystallisation and metal fatigue-leading to breakage. For example, cast steel spindles which have been heated can shatter on impact! The workmanship involved in so-called repairs of this sort is often of a quality which can only be described as horrifying!
They also go on to talk about the extent of the problem and they sort of ask rhetorically:
Are these examples of shoddy workmanship simply isolated incidents? Just how serious can these shoddy repairs be? Why is this problem receiving so much attention now?
The answers to these questions have a common bond: the changing technology used in the manufacture of today's automobiles.
As oil prices climbed in the early 1970s, auto manufacturers scrambled to produce smaller and more fuel efficient automobiles. Engineers developed new models which employed front wheel drive technology, used high-strength low-alloy steel in structural components and utilized "unibody" or "monococque" construction.
Ibday's automobile is a radical departure from those found on our highways even 10 years ago!
Those that I suspect all of us at one time tinkered with in our backyards trying to keep them on the road.
No longer are we seeing the classic sedan, with its frame construction and heavy sheet metal panels. Today's car employs unibody construction, with no frame in the traditional sense and with considerably lighter sheet metal. With unibody cars, the sheet metal is attached to a subframe and the subframe and sheet metal form the "unibody". This represents the structural integrity of the vehicle.
Tolerances are more closely defined. Repair technicians must now work to tolerances that are within millimetres-with little room for error!
Many collision shops have made large investments in sophisticated measuring and pulling equipment, which allows them to repair vehicles to tolerances defined by the manufacturers. The extensive use of high-strength low-alloy steels has necessitated the use of Mig welding equipment, to retain the integrity of these critical components after welding.
Unfortunately, most amateur rebuilders possess neither the equipment nor the training necessary to properly repair today's unibody vehicles. When proper techniques and procedures are not used in the repair of these highly sophisticated automobiles, the result is often a vehicle which could be described as a potential "death trap"!

March 29, 1993
Government Orders
We saw some examples of that. One of the witnesses came before the committee with a video tape of a 60 Minutes program. They had taken a crew to a number of automobile retail outlets in the United States where people were buying cars that in fact were two cars. The cars had been wrecked, the front end had been chopped off and another one welded in its place. These were totally unsafe vehicles. They were not telling their customers that these had been recycled vehicles. In fact it was shown on the tape that people were saying: "It has never been scratched. It has never been repainted". It was more than scratched and it was more than repainted. It was totally rebuilt using the front end of one car and the back end of another. That is the kind of vehicle we are concerned about.
I certainly know from the testimony we heard that members on all sides of the committee were quite concerned about what was happening. But they were also frustrated that we as a federal Parliament could only do so much and that it was really up to our provincial and territorial colleagues to put in place the kind of legislative regime that is possible.
The province of Quebec has a regime in place. If you take a vehicle to the motor licensing branch of the province of Quebec, if it is a used vehicle you have to bring with you a picture that shows it has been examined on a full body frame. That is a special piece of equipment which is available in body shops. The licensing branch knows that it has been inspected by a qualified body mechanic who has an understanding of the structural integrity of the vehicle and therefore can indicate whether the vehicle has been recycled.
We need to have that kind of approach adopted right across the country. I would encourage the Minister of Transport to press his provincial colleagues through the committee of the Canadian Council of Motor Transport Administrators to do that very thing, to really accelerate their work. They will be meeting some time in the next month or two to accelerate their work and to bring together a national standard.
Certainly we have seen in the area of the environment where the federal government has adopted a policy after consultation with the provinces and then the provinces have enacted it in law.
It is important that we do that. It is important that all members in this House contact their respective provincial ministers of transport to put pressure on them to go along.
Finally, and I know I only have one minute, there are a number of other areas where the federal government can take a lead. For example, although it does not have legal jurisdiction there could be a national data bank to which all provinces could send their vehicle registration information and where all police departments could easily pull it out.
We need to work with the provinces to ensure that the environmental controls we put in cars are maintained because at the federal level we can only decide what the starting quality is. We have no jurisdiction on ensuring that they are repaired and maintained. That is up to the provinces. We need a national standard so that we can adopt basically what B.C. has done in terms of its clean air controls and its mandatory inspections, as I understand it, of pollution equipment.
There is a lot more work to be done. My compliments to my colleagues on the committee and my compliments to the government for its willingness to address these areas.

speechtext: that Bill C-116, an act to provide for greater certainty in the reconciliation of the personal interests and duties of office of public office holders, to establish a Conflict of Interests Commission, to amend the Parliament of Canada Act and to make consequential amendments to other acts, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Departmental envelope.

subtopic: CONFLICT OF INTERESTS OF PUBLIC OFFICE HOLDERS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise on the second reading of Bill C-116, an act to provide for greater certainty in the reconciliation of the personal interests and duties of public office holders, to establish a Conflict of Interests Commission, to amend the Parliament of Canada Act and to make consequential amendments to other acts.
As hon. members will know the bill is really a response to the joint committee's report on conflict of interest that was received by the government in June. That was a unanimous committee report of the Senate and the House working together. This bill to a large extent reflects the unanimity of that committee report.
Each one of us understands the task before us is important, not only because of the direct impact this proposed legislation will have on us personally as parliamentarians but also because of its implications for the operation of parliamentary government in Canada.
Government Orders
As parliamentarians we have all sought office in this place for one principal reason: to serve the interests of Canadians so that their hopes and desires and those of their children and their children's children are properly and fully realized.
It has been sadly unfashionable and all too common to criticize and call into question the motives of politicians. Unfortunately there are always some people who abuse public office for their own personal gain and do not live up to the trust bestowed upon them when they are elected or appointed to public office. These few individuals are rightly the object of public criticism and censure.
It is nevertheless distressing to all of us as parliamentarians to work within an environment where every action we take as we carry on the duties of our offices is subject to scrutiny in the expectation that we are sinners and we are going to do something wrong and that in everything we do we are hiding something. That is the reason for this legislation.
The problem of conflict of interest is a perennial one. It dates back to the origins of democracy itself. There were such problems in ancient Greece and Rome. These difficulties have persisted over the centuries. Nonetheless the problem of conflict of interest is perennial as are our obligations to overcome it.
Political leaders if they are to act effectively must have and deserve to have the trust and confidence of the people they represent. This trust, which is not to be given lightly, can only be fostered in a political situation where there is a system of openness and accountability.
All the players in such a system must know and understand the rules of the game. The rules therefore must be as straightforward and as direct as possible. To illustrate this point I will use an analogy which Canadians will understand.
Conflict of interest rules should be like the rules in the game of football. Everyone who enters public life seeks to reach and cross over the goal line at the end of his or her career. The goal to which we aspire is to carry out one's duties of office fully, effectively and responsibly and conclude one's career on a high note without becoming involved in conflicts of interest, without casting doubt on one's motives and intentions, without

March 29, 1993
Government Orders
ruining one's good name and reputation or that of one's colleagues.
Unfortunately over the years the playing-field has become more complex and the yardsticks keep moving. We often find that our job is to represent Canadians in a responsible manner but we are often attacked as we carry out those responsibilities. As parliamentarians we are busy people with many responsibilities and demands on our time. In such an atmosphere it is often difficult to be aware and reflect on every nuance of a situation to make sure that no conflict might arise.
However we all understand that constant vigilance is required to ensure that we know and understand the rules that will help us avoid conflicts of interest so that we do not stray out of bounds. We must always be scrupulous because the penalties are very onerous. The loss of reputation alone is a very strong incentive not to become involved in a situation where one's conduct of public office or behaviour can be called into question.
Parliament has learned about that reality over the years and in particular about what will and will not be tolerated by Canadians in public life.
The boundaries of the political playing field have become more apparent and real to all of us because of what we have learned and understood from the shortcomings which act as lessons of what not to do.
The bill before us today is intended to make those lines even clearer and to give all members of Parliament, senators, ministers and parliamentary secretaries mechanisms to assist them to keep their personal affairs in order so that these personal concerns will not interfere with their public responsibilities.
In tabling the legislation the government realizes that proposed legislation is not perfect and that Parliament has an important responsibility to examine it carefully to determine if any improvements are required.
Government welcomes the process because government wants more than anything else for Parliament to give this whole problem its greatest and fullest consideration. This is so that Parliament can produce a piece of legislation as quickly as possible on this most important public matter.
Before we begin this work I would like to therefore describe briefly the main provisions of the bill and its importance.
We are aware that very high standards of public conduct are rightfully expected by parliamentarians from all Canadians. Upholding the public trust is a clear priority of this bill. An illustration of this commitment is the obligation of parliamentarians, ministers and parliamentary secretaries listed in the purpose clauses in both parts of the bill. I want to say at this stage that unlike the parliamentary committee report the bill is a two-stage bill. There is a stage of the bill designed for ministers and parliamentary secretaries and the Order in Council appointments made by the cabinet of senior public servants, deputy ministers and the like. That part of the bill goes to a commission and the commission reports to the Prime Minister. The reason for that is that the Prime Minister is responsible and the officials, his parliamentary secretaries and ministers, are responsible to him. He has to make sure that their conduct is above reproach. He has a commission to look after that and it is separate from the actions of parliamentarians, senators and ordinary members of Parliament.
Ordinary members of Parliament will report to a jurisconsult. The jurisconsult will be a person to whom they can report their activities and who will look after their conflicts and who will adjudicate their concerns and will report to the Speaker. The jurisconsult reports to the Speaker who reports to Parliament. The commission reports to the Prime Minister.
Both sections of the statute are similar. In both sections the standard under which people are judged is essentially the same. There are rules which govern parliamentarians in both Houses. Both parts of the bill make it clear that no parliamentarian should advance his or her private interests or those of a spouse or dependents on the basis of information that is not available to the public or use his or her influence to obtain by reason of public office a personal benefit or personal gain.
Both parts of the bill have rules of disclosure of gifts and benefits which will apply to all members, senators, ministers and parliamentary secretaries and of course
March 29, 1993

Government Orders
those other persons who are covered by the bill in terms of the commission part of the bill.
All members and ministers and parliamentary secretaries are required to admit to meet basic requirements; to report and disclose their private interests and those of their spouses and dependents to either the jurisconsult in the case of members and senators and to the conflict of interest commission with respect to parliamentary secretaries and ministers; to establish in conjunction with either the jurisconsult or the commission a personally tailored regime taking into account their responsibilities for arranging their assets to avoid conflict; and finally to prepare a public declaration of these interests as either the jurisconsult or the commission sees fit and, in the case of spouses and dependents, relevant.
These rules reflect the political reality that any member of Parliament, senator, minister or parliamentary secretary can appear to have or actually be involved in a conflict of interest. The bill, therefore, represents a comprehensive approach to the ethics of parliamentarians and public office holders and will ensure that Canadians can have confidence in all of their representations.
I should, however, point out that the bill provides that ministers and parliamentary secretaries must satisfy more stringent requirements because of the positions they hold. The government recognizes that potential for conflict of interest is greater for ministers and parliamentary secretaries than for regular members and senators.
Accordingly those who hold these offices will have to disclose their private interests and, where the commission deems it necessary, make a public declaration according to stricter standards than members and senators.
In addition, ministers and parliamentary secretaries will not be permitted to engage in any employment, business or in the practice of a profession outside their official duties. Ministers and parliamentary secretaries will not be permitted to accept any fees.
Finally there are specific rules on post-employment which will apply to ministers and parliamentary secretaries but of course not to parliamentarians.
These different requirements for ministers and parliamentary secretaries reflect the political reality that those members of the ministry exercise broader responsibilities of office and could experience opportunities for influence that do not go beyond those of private members and senators.
I want to take the opportunity in this context to discuss another important aspect of the bill that has in the past given legitimate concern. It is the requirement that spouses and dependents participate on the same terms as members and ministers in relation to the disclosure of their private interests and the treatment of gifts, personal benefits and hospitality which they receive.
The government does not view spouses as mere appendages. The government thinks that the disclosure to the jurisconsult or the commission of private interests required in respect of a spouse might be identical in scope to that required of a member or public office holder.
This is a recognition of the reality that marriage is an economic partnership and that husbands and wives have a direct pecuniary interest in each other's financial affairs.
I want to say though that this matter was a key issue in the debate of the committee. As far as the members and senators are concerned, the disclosure of what is the interest of a spouse will be made by the member or the senator to the jurisconsult. The spouse will not be required to file anything with respect to a minister or parliamentary secretary, on the other hand, because of the higher degree of responsibility. One does not have to accept a ministry or accept being a parliamentary secretary. A spouse will be required to disclose to the commission. The spouse does not have to disclose to the member but they have to disclose in that case to the commission.
This is a difficult and very exacerbating field. The joint committee had a number of sessions and heard a number of representations on the matter. I think that the committee will examine that issue again. I think the committee will find that this way of approaching it is probably realistic.

March 29, 1993
Government Orders
The declaration by the member with respect to his or her spouse's assets to a jurisconsult is fine but when it comes to a minister or parliamentary secretary then a separate declaration is important.
In extending the provisions of the bill the government wants to preserve as far as possible the privacy of spouses and their dependents. I think particularly as we move forward with a society where both spouses have their own separate and independent careers that it is important that this conflict of interest bill protects the independence of spouses.
We will perhaps have to examine the legislation again. I believe that the bill sets forth a pretty good regime. It is on that basis that the government has put it forward.
The bill is really an attempt to have the jurisconsult and the commission balance the public interest in disclosure with the right of the minister or private member to privacy and to safeguard against unnecessary public disclosure. After all there is no need for people to know exactly whether one has 100 shares of the Bell Telephone Company or 1,000 as long as you do not have a controlling, significant or major interest. These are very small amounts. To say that a person has a minor interest in certain shares was judged to be sufficient by the committee that reported.
The question of what is disclosed will be in the hands of the commission and the jurisconsult that will make public disclosure. That public disclosure will be available for those who really want to read it.
The concept is that the commission and the jurisconsult will make sure that the public has confidence that members, ministers, parliamentary secretaries and senators are not hiding something, that they are not trying to feather their nests by hiding that nest somewhere. It will be disclosed because disclosure really represents the essence of control on conflict of interest.
My remarks are relatively short today. I believe we can move this bill forward. We intend to have a committee study it in joint consultation with the Senate. It is important that the matter move forward as quickly as possible through the House so that we can get going on the committee work.
It is no secret that this Parliament is drawing to a close. I believe it is absolutely essential that this legislation be in place before the next Parliament. Therefore we have to move ahead. That being the case, I am going to turn the floor over to someone else to make a speech on the matter and perhaps we can get it completed today.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: CONFLICT OF INTERESTS OF PUBLIC OFFICE HOLDERS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate.
As the Official Opposition critic for government operations I want to indicate that this bill is very long awaited. This is a debate which I had hoped we would have had long ago. I am pleased that we are finally having it today.
I want to indicate that on behalf of my colleagues we have no intention at all of delaying this bill. We want it to go to committee as early as possible. We want to co-operate because we feel this issue is important.
I am one of those who believes that what we do as legislators does not only consist of the bills that we pass, it consists largely in the trust that Canadians have in those who occupy the seats in this great institution.

The hon. Leader of the Opposition, in a speech he gave over a year ago right here in Ottawa at the Congress Centre, when he asked me to prepare a report on public morality, told us how proud he was the day he was elected to Parliament. He told us about his father's even greater pride in seeing this son, the 18th of his 19 children, which the Leader of the Opposition is, elected to the House of Commons. The father of the member for Beausejour felt this great honour and pride.
March 29, 1993

The member for Beausejour wondered whether his father would feel as proud today, given the debates that have gone on in recent years. He concluded that unfortunately his father probably would not feel so proud, but that it was important to restore the pride people once had in our parliamentary institutions. That is what the Leader of the Opposition said and I agree with him.
Mr. Diefenbaker, a former Prime Minister, some years ago said that there was no greater honour for a Canadian than to be elected by his or her fellow citizens to sit in this, the highest court in the land, the Parliament of Canada. How true that is.
When I was elected on September 4, 1984 how special that day was for me. A week or so later when I came to Parliament Hill, I walked in through the main entrance, the one under the Peace Tower. For me that was symbolically important because, as you may know, I had been a staffer on Parliament Hill. I do not know whether that is still the case, although I should know, but as a staffer there was one entrance that we were prohibited from using. It is not permitted for a staffer here to use the main entrance to Parliament, the one under the Peace Tower.
The day after I was elected it was a special privilege for me to walk in through that entrance, and I walked across that threshold into Parliament as an MP.
Notwithstanding some of the things that have happened over recent years, I still feel this way about this great institution. Perhaps in my case being an MP was a boyhood dream. It is ironic that I came into this building for the first time not as an MP but as a busboy in the parliamentary restaurant. I worked my way up a number of rungs in the ladder, was elected to municipal office and then to the provincial legislature of Ontario. I resigned my position here when I was elected to Queen's Park.
I came back in 1984 to become an MP in this same building where I had once served as a busboy in the parliamentary restaurant. Maybe that even adds more to my pride in the great privilege that was given me by the
Government Orders
electors of the great riding of Glengarry-Prescott- Russell.
It is important for all of us collectively and individually to do everything we can to restore confidence in this great place. I will not go into all the things that have happened because I do not think today is the day that we should have that partisan speech. I make it often enough when it is my role to question the government on various issues.
Today is the day we should all be getting together to ensure that we do whatever it takes to amend our rules, yes, but also to ensure that those who will be elected in the next Parliament, and those who are here now who will continue to serve in the next Parliament, will do their best to restore integrity in Parliament. That is the first premise. That is what all this is about.
Here we have Bill C-116. How did we get started on a conflict of interest bill? Well, you will remember, Mr. Speaker, that we had a set of rules better known as the conflict of interest guidelines.

In 1985 the Prime Minister replaced these rules with a conflict of interest code. In 1987, unfortunately as a result of the circumstances surrounding the resignation of a minister, Judge Parker recommended that Parliament pass a law. I have here the report of the Parker Commission which recommended conflict of interest legislation for the Parliament of Canada. Of course Judge Parker made several other recommendations and concluded that the minister in question had broken the rules many times, 14 times, if I remember correctly.
For the purposes of our discussion today it is important to note that as the starting point for having a law.

This bill is actually our fourth tentative try at conflict of interest rules. I believe the first bill was Bill C-46, the second one Bill C-114, and the third one Bill C-43.
I must say in retrospect, and I share these comments with the member from Mississauga South, that I am glad Bill C-43 as originally drafted was never enacted because some of its provisions were outright ridiculous. Frankly, I do not know how it was put together but it could not have worked. I am not even sure that it would have

March 29, 1993
Government Orders
accomplished what we were trying to do in the first place. Certain of its provisions were absurdly strict and in other areas it did not even do the job.
Our committee looked at that. When I say our committee I mean the committee under the co-chairmanship of the member for Mississauga South and Senator Stanbury, a member of the other place. We had extensive deliberations and it is important for the House and all Canadians to know that we came up with a unanimous report.
It does not mean that everything in the report was the absolute best and what I wanted. I guess the same could be said for the member for Mississauga South or the member for Oshawa. It means that there are some things on which we could unanimously agree, and at least we made those kinds of agreements.
I want to refer to a few things in the bill, notwithstanding my agreement with the bill in general, which I hope we will seek to amend at committee.
First of all, there is a drafting error in the title of the bill. The bill is referred to as the Conflict of Interest of Public Office Holders Act. While of course the member for Mississauga South, the member for Oshawa and I are not public office holders, we are parliamentarians. Because we are not public office holders, the bill should be renamed and the word parliamentarian has to be added to that because it is wrong just from that standpoint.
There are certain provisions in the bill that I would like to see changed slightly, for example the two-year purgatory for civil servants and public office holders generally to lobby their own departments. Under the bill that is proposed it is to be shortened to one year. I know it was the unanimous recommendation of our committee, but we proposed to shorten that to one year and at the same time we proposed to keep the clause whereby cabinet can shorten it even more. The combination of the two means that in many cases the cooling off period or purgatory could effectively disappear.
We should make a choice whether we keep one year hard and fast. I do not think that is the best way. I think the best way is to have it two years with a possible application for exceptional circumstances which is what is there now. That gives a little bit more flexibility, yet gives a cooling off period that will be seen by the public,
and will be in reality as well as one which is more meaningful.
I also want to say a word here to those members of this place who serve on the Board of Internal Economy and perhaps to our good clerks at the table because I understand that they are also clerks of the Committee of Internal Economy.
I think it would be important for us as parliamentarians as we start our committee work to ensure that the definitions that we use in the bill are similar to those used by the Board of Internal Economy. For instance, the definition of a spouse in the bill and the definition of a spouse as the Board of Internal Economy sees it for benefits of parliamentarians and so on is not exactly the same.
We should do our best to ensure that there is uniformity all the way through in both Bill C-116, our conflict of interest act, and the rules as administered by the House and perhaps by the other place as well.
The committee has not yet been officially named, but I hope to be a member of the committee. If we had that, as members of the committee we could have those definitions and reconcile them in the best way to ensure that we have workable legislation.
I guess I have officially informed you, Mr. Speaker, that I would hope the Board of Internal Economy would do this. Perhaps our good clerks could take note of that and consult the Speaker about it. I for one would love to have that kind of information. It would assist me in doing my work as a member of that committee. I hope to be a member of the committee.
This bill is not quite the same as our report. The member across the way has identified the major changes. First, as we will all know, we agreed in our committee that instead of conflict of interest rules administered by an officer of Parliament, known as a jurisconsult, there should be four MPs and senators. That is what is in the bill.
On the other hand, we also agreed that we need other rules for the Order in Council appointments administered by the government.
In the middle is another group of people. They are the public office holders who sit in Parliament, namely the cabinet ministers and the parliamentary secretaries.

What do you do with them? They could go either way because they are both public office holders and they are parliamentarians.
We thought in our committee that they should be dealt with by the officer of Parliament. The government in producing the bill says no, we will put him in the other category. As I say, I do not think I am married to that principle but I do have a concern. The concern is more particularly with the parliamentary secretaries. There are a few of them sitting in the House as we are speaking now.
I see our colleague from Burlington. I think he is a parliamentary secretary. He will understand that parliamentary secretaries tend to change perhaps more quickly than ministers. If you have a parliamentary secretary who will go into that parliamentary secretaryship, if I can call it that, and out of it, and perhaps change over many times in the term of a Parliament that person could have the rules that apply to him administered by the jurisconsult and the conflict of interest commission and his or her file could be going back and forth between the two officers depending on how often he or she enters or leaves the parliamentary secretary position.
You could almost have someone walking back and forth with boxes of files between the officer of Parliament, the jurisconsult, and the commission that will be dealing with the conflict of interest for the public office holders. There is an area there which is of concern to me as to how that will apply.
I have another area of concern as well. Because we are going to have both a commission and a jurisconsult, what happens in the event that someone receives a punishment? For the purpose of my argument, we have a minister who receives or is subjected to some sort of punishment from the Prime Minister pursuant to something that was declared to be improper by the commission. Does that mean that the jurisconsult cannot have a parallel inquiry of the same individual because the individual in addition to being a minister is also a member of Parliament?
What happens in those cases? I am a little unclear as to that. The bill does not describe it well enough or I have not been briefed well enough. I am concerned about what could happen in those cases.

I think the member for Mississauga South will agree with me that there are areas where it could be confusing at best. I hope that officials from the justice department or wherever who are taking notes as we are debating this will note and as much as possible address them when they come to speak at our committee to ensure that we do not have someone either being- pardon the expression but it is not quite that- almost tried twice for the same offence using two different court systems.
Also there are grey areas in a case where a person was a public office holder and may have committed an offence at the time that he was a public office holder but the offence is discovered by the jurisconsult when he ceased to be a public office holder.
I do not know how that will work. I do not want to throw a can of worms in all of this. I only want to indicate to my colleagues areas of concern so that we can improve the bill and have it work as well as possible.
I want to say a word as well on spousal declarations. Here I am going to give a personal view. My view is that for individual MPs and cabinet ministers it should be obligatory for the spouse to register. That is my personal view and I am going to leave it at that.
I accept what has been decided, that in the case of a parliamentarian the parliamentarian reports incomes and so on for the spouse to the best of his or her ability. If his knowledge of the spouse's interest is negligible we are not going to get much. As I say it is with reluctance that I accept that, great reluctance.
In the case of a cabinet minister it becomes obligatory. That has to be paramount. The reason that is important is the following: We are all here today as members of Parliament. If new rules are applied to us while we are already here as MPs in the case of a cabinet minister it is going to be very easy to make the decision I think. The day after the next election when the new government is elected, and needless to say I hope it is a government led by the now member for Beausejour, soon to be member for Shawinigan and Prime Minister, he may phone a colleague of mine, say the member for Saint-Leonard, and says he would like that member to be a cabinet minister. The member for Saint-Leonard can say he would like to take a moment to discuss it with his spouse to see if they are both willing to file the conflict of interest forms. If one of the two refuses to sign the member can then say: "Sorry, Leader, some other time".

March 29, 1993
Government Orders
If they both agree that that is going to be the rule then they live by it.
That is why I think it is particularly important for those who are public office holders to be subjected to that kind of rule. I happen to think, and perhaps I am a voice in the wilderness, that should apply to all MPs and senators as well, but I will leave it at that.
In order to ensure that everyone can live with these rules I have a suggestion. Make the date of proclamation the date of the next election. If someone cannot live with these rules they can pack it in and go home. We can say we do not want them here if they cannot live with the rules. They cannot say they were applied retroactively and they did not know about them when they came here. If you cannot live with the rule then go home. If you can live with the rule run again, be a candidate. When you come here, prior to being sworn in as an MP or within the requisite time after, file the appropriate declarations so that Canadians know that at least there is that level of good faith in living within the rules.
Let there be no mistake. Conflict of interest rules in themselves do not necessarily mean good behaviour.
What you need first and foremost is good intention. I am sure most of us have good intention, but I hope that all of us have the intention to live with these rules.
Some may ask: Is it going to be hard to recruit candidates having these rules? Justice Parker addressed that in the report in which he said that the Centre for Responsive Politics in the United States had undertaken a study of this issue some time ago.
What the centre discovered at the time was that in fact stricter rules actually attracted, by and large, better candidates because people knew that they would be sitting in a parliament or in a legislative body together with other people who were willing to live under tougher rules and who had the intention, at least stated, of living under those rules.
Therefore, Justice Parker had concluded that you are not going to have a problem finding good candidates if you have tougher rules. Providing that the rules are reasonable, you may find it easier. I have just found a
quote here from page 350 of the Parker commission of inquiry report. It said:
I was particularly interested to learn that the disclosure requirements have not discouraged "good people" from entering politics or running for public office. For example, a study of members of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate conducted by the Centre for Responsive Politics in 1985 found no one who felt that financial disclosure affected his or her decision to seek public office.
Even having said that, it does not mean that we can make all kinds of unreasonable rules. I see our colleague from Oshawa here today. He has served and so have I in another legislative assembly, namely the Legislative Assembly of the Province of Ontario.
I know he chaired a committee after I left which dealt with an issue involving the financial interests of a certain cabinet minister. He and I have talked about it in the past. While I will not pretend to speak for him at this moment, the job of serving on the committee reviewing that was no picnic. I do not think that the member for Oshawa would be the first to rush in and volunteer his services to sit on a committee like that again after the experience that he lived through.
It is tough to sit on a committee involving disciplining one's own peers. It is not something that members will be rushing out to perform. It is a difficult task, perhaps a necessary one. I think the experience of our colleague from Oshawa is rather unique in this Chamber. I look forward to the contribution that he will be providing to our committee.
He has the option of giving us sober second thought from the House because he has dealt with this issue before having chaired such a committee in the Ontario legislature.
I want to take two minutes and speak about those who have said that this bill is a watered down bill on conflict of interest. I beg to differ. This is not watered down compared to the present conflict of interest code. No way. This is as strict and certainly much stricter in the case of MPs. They are not even affected by the present code.
Some will say: "Oh yes, but it is watered down compared to Bill C-43". Some provisions did not make sense, perhaps. Over all, no, it is not watered down. I submit it is not.
March 29, 1993

Let me give an example of a clause of Bill C-43.1 will give this one from personal experience because when I read the bill the first time it struck me rather strongly. Bill C-43 said that every time a spouse of a parliamentarian received a fee the spouse would then have to disclose that to the jurisconsult. I looked at my own situation. In my wife's job she does not get a salary, she gets fees. That means every time she received her paycheque she would have to come and register. She is a real estate agent, and as such she is paid fees. I understand that the same would apply to lawyers and perhaps many other professions as well. In the case of people who are even more active in private enterprise they could be registering daily.
What would that have accomplished?
