There we go. My colleague from Saint-Leonard says his wife is an accountant. She would probably have been one of those people registering daily because every time one fills out somebody's income tax form one is paid a fee, not a salary. Therefore she would have been registering all the time.
There were major errors in Bill C-43 and we have corrected them. That does not mean we have watered down the bill. I hope it means we have corrected some of the mistakes. That does not mean that this bill does not have mistakes. We will discover things that are wrong with it at committee. I am sure we will and I hope we do. If we do we will have an opportunity to improve the bill.
Even with everyone's best intentions I am sure there will be mistakes after we have gone through the bill. Hopefully the next Parliament can correct those as time goes by. Perhaps we should do what was done with the Lobbyists Registration Act and have a three-year review put into the bill. We did that with the Lobbyists Registration Act. It was a triggering mechanism that incited all of us to look at the bill again. That is not a bad idea and possibly those of us who hopefully will be reviewing this bill at committee level should consider that.
I want to conclude my remarks on that by thanking my colleagues who served on the committee that produced the report on Bill C-43. I also want to indicate that my
Government Orders
colleague from Saint-Denis will be speaking shortly. He has given an immense contribution because although he is not the dean of MPs he is the next one to it. He has been here the second longest of all MPs in the House. He is more experienced than many of us, even though he is still a very young MP of course. He will be proud to read in Hansard that I said that about him. The member for Saint-Denis has been an MP for a very long time and his contribution at the committee level was quite impressive and will continue to be. Many members, and members of the other place as well, made excellent contributions at the committee level.
I want to close by thanking the member for Beausejour for making this issue an important one for our party. I happen to think that the issue of reconciling members' interests and the trust that we have in this institution is important for us. I want to thank the member for Beausejour, the Leader of the Liberal Party, for having identified that issue as being a priority issue for him. I say the same as well to the member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, who is the House leader and ultimately has many decisions to make in terms of the interventions we make on various issues, and the Whip, the member for Saint-Leonard, who permitted me to be one of the Liberal members doing the report on Bill C-43. I appreciated that opportunity as well.

I want to say to all hon. members that we must not let this bill die on the Order Paper of the House of Commons. I think we have a duty not to rush this bill through without examining it because it is an important bill, but to give it thorough consideration immediately within the next few days or weeks and to report back to the House before Parliament adjourns in June.
I expect, as do other members, that when Parliament adjourns in June for the summer recess, there will no further sitting of this Parliament. There will be an election so I do not think we will come back in the fall. According to most parliamentarians, Parliament will not come back in the fall and an election will be called. It is important for us all to adopt this bill so the next Parliament will have an instrument that will prove to be very useful for parliamentarians.

March 29, 1993

As I said earlier, good rules do not necessarily guarantee good behaviour. Idle rules however are there to help us and, more importantly, to restore the confidence of Canadians in this great parliamentary institution, the highest court in the land, the Parliament of Canada.

subtopic: CONFLICT OF INTERESTS OF PUBLIC OFFICE HOLDERS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say that we support the principle of this bill. We had a little bit of discussion back and forth about how quickly it ought to be processed. The only thing I would like to say on that is that it deserves due consideration by all the members here. It is not something that should be done quickly. It should not be a one-day wonder but it should not be stalled either.
It should have a reasonable amount of debate. For our part, we have two speakers on second reading. We would be quite happy to go off and work through the committee stage of the bill. For what it is worth, I believe, as others have already said, that this is a bill that ought to be completed some time before the end of June and it ought to be in place and in operation before the next election is held.
I want to start by doing something I never do. I want to thank the member for Mississauga South and Senator Stanbuiy, in the other place, for restoring my faith in the fact that this process works, as someone who has been in politics for a while but is new to this place.
I was somewhat taken aback by what I saw here in my first year or so. It struck me that much of what happens here is not very productive and is not very useful to the Canadian people. In fact, it is downright stupid.
In sitting on this joint committee I had my faith in the parliamentary process renewed somewhat because I found there people from all political parties, from the two Houses, who did what I think Parliaments are supposed to do. They sat down, looked at the problem and tried to find a reasoned and reasonable solution to it. That does not always happen in Parliaments. Sometimes Parliaments do particularly silly and stupid things. Watching this place on television it is sometimes hard to explain just exactly what is going on here at any given moment.
One of the tragedies is that while people see Question Period on television, which I am kind of ashamed of, they
did not get to see the work of this committee, which is what a Parliament really does.
Conflict of interest legislation seems to bring out the best and the worst in people. I do not know why that is. For all those who have a tendency to be pompous, it seems to bring out the absolute worst in them. They give great speeches about the integrity of public office holders and how wonderful everybody who ever got elected is, how they have no faults, how they live hard lives, everybody makes great sacrifices and what a noble privilege it is to serve.
I have been in politics for 20 years at every level and I do not subscribe to any of that. People in public life are people first and last: good ones and bad ones, smart ones and stupid ones, honest ones and dishonest ones, and people who work hard and people who do not deserve five cents for their day's work. They are people and they are in a sense what the original Parliament was on the fields of Runnymede. At Runnymede it was a good idea to watch where one was stepping because it was an open field. They came there on horseback. It is my experience today in any Parliament that I have ever seen that it is not a bad idea to keep an eye peeled for meadow muffins because they are still there. In part that is what conflict of interest legislation is about.
For many in the public I suppose the impression is left that all one has to do is pass a bill like this and all the problems are resolved. I think those of us who have been in politics for a while know that that is not very close to the truth at all. This bill for example does not stop any criminal allegations against anybody nor should it. If somebody is elected and breaks the law then they should expect and get no favour from anybody. They should be treated before the courts of Canada as any other citizen would be treated. This bill is not about that kind of activity. If someone steals or commits a crime under the Criminal Code of Canada then they should be treated exactly the same as every other Canadian citizen. That is the first thing that I think needs to be put on the record.
A conflict of interest bill at its very best tries to define the grey areas of politics. Where did someone exercise a little undue influence? Just exactly how did they do that? Of course it is almost impossible. As someone who chaired a committee at the Ontario legislature and studied every conceivable version of conflict of interest
March 29, 1993

legislation, there are all kinds of varieties out there and none seem to do the job much better than any other.
Some jurisdictions I have looked at put a heavy emphasis on paperwork. They seemingly believe that if one fills boxes and boxes of declarations about this and bank accounts about the relatives doing likewise then somehow that alleviates conflict of interest. I do not think it does.
Some jurisdictions that I looked at really went in hot and heavy for great police investigations. In the United States for example it is fairly common practice to have the FBI, the CIA and everybody else go out and conduct field interviews. In other words if one is accused of something or going to be appointed to some great office in the United States then it is common practice that the FBI will knock on the door of your neighbours and ask what kind of a person you are. That information is gathered and then put into files. The files are shown to some members of Congress and not necessarily to others. We have all managed to watch televised proceedings of some of their hearing processes where the flavour of all this kind of comes out. Does it result in a better system than what is proposed here? I am not sure that it does. It certainly has to be more expensive but I am not sure it provides a better system.
Some would advocate that a great bureaucracy should be built up to examine the records of all members of Parliament, everybody who is a parliamentary secretary and everybody who is in the cabinet. I am not sure what useful purpose would be served by that.
I do know this. What has happened in this House is almost the same as what I have seen in every other jurisdiction. Parliaments and legislatures do this kind of stuff reluctantly. It is usually after there have been a series of allegations laid against the members. Frankly it is not usually the ones where there are Criminal Code violations that cause the problem because generally the courts pick that up, go to work and do their job as they normally would. It is the grey areas of influence peddling and who helped make some decision and might profit by that. Allegations in Ontario led to that law. I am
Government Orders
someone who chaired one of the committees that heard the conflict of interest allegations there.
It kind of comes down to this: A gentleman who was a good friend of mine was a minister of natural resources and he wrote cutting licences for timber firms in northern Ontario. He happened to belong to a family that operated a lumber company in northern Ontario in Kapuskasing. He sat down beside me on the first day and said privately: "Mike, what was I supposed to do? My family runs the only lumber company in town. I am the minister. Why would I not sign the licences? I did not make any money off that". On the last day of the hearings he said much the same thing to me. I do not think he got the message all the way through.
The husband of another friend of mine borrowed some money from the Government of Ontario and she was in charge of a ministry that administered those funds. She did not see the conflict either.
In my household, and I suspect in most, if my spouse borrowed a million dollars and I did not know about it then there would be more than a conflict of interest involved in this. If I borrowed a million dollars and did not go home and tell my spouse about it then there would be a little discussion at the Breaugh's kitchen table that night. However, not every household is the same. Part of what a conflict of interest bill has to try to do is to take the perception of everybody and find a way to sort it all out. Very often the perception of a conflict of interest is just as important as an actual conflict of interest. In other words, it really does not matter if somebody made a million dollars that they should not have. If the rest of the world thinks they made a million dollars then it hurts the process.
It hurts the process in this way. All members of this Chamber are damaged when an allegation is made that somebody here made some money that they should not have. That is unfair. We all know that. There is something that I think is true when those allegations are raised. I have had some interesting discussions over the years with colleagues who love to make these allegations. I have often said: "Do you know that something is wrong here?" They would say: "It sure looks like there is

March 29, 1993
Government Orders
something fishy". The end result was: "Let's go fishing and see if we can destroy somebody's reputation". I am not so sure that is a useful exercise for anybody.
One of the reasons that I am an advocate of conflict of interest legislation is that in my books and having studied it in a number of places there are some simple, straightforward things that have to be done. First and foremost there has to be a law such as the one that is being proposed here. Rightly or wrongly and whether it is imperfect or not, at least it lays down in legal form what is expected of the members.
Never mind the rules or guidelines or advisers. Never mind how fancy it gets. What I want is a law. If one believes in it then write it down. That law in my books should be put together in somewhat the way this one was. I am choosing my words a little carefully here.
Say the government had said: "We have had a special joint committee of the House and the Senate study it and draft a bill". Then it brought that bill in here. I would say the obligation is on the members here to read the bill, to understand it, to know what it means and go forward with it. That is exactly the way I think it should be done.
This bill was not done quite that way. I want to make this distinction. This bill is based in part on the report of the joint committee and in part from somewhere else. Most notably I would ascribe it to the cabinet submission called Bill C-43 which was brought forward previously. That is I think one of the problems. The good side is that there is now a law being proposed.
The second thing-I think most experts in the field would advocate this-is some form of disclosure. What do I mean by disclosure? It is public disclosure in particular. It gets a little sticky. It is not quite as simple as it first appears. There is no polite way to say this. Members ought to have a public record of what they own and what their interests are. I have done that and other members in this Chamber have done that in other places at other times. It is no big deal for most of us. For those of us for whom it is a big deal, it is probably even more important that they do a public disclosure statement because they will have more opportunities and more areas where disclosure could be found.
My experience in Ontario unfortunately was this. We insisted on disclosure on a fairly broad basis by every single member of the House. The first year those disclosure reports were made public the press wrote
reams of stories. They were not all factual, sensible or worth really writing about but they wrote them anyway. The news was that here is public disclosure on Ontario's politicians. The second year they wrote a few less stories. By about the third year it hit the norm.
The purpose of the exercise is not to provide The Toronto Sun or The Ottawa Sun with new fodder for columns. It ought to be to provide the public with some access point where they can find out where there might be conflicts for the members. This is a little stickier that it first appears to be.
There is the matter of privacy for the members and privacy for their spouses. I would advocate that somebody who is not elected to this place-a male or female spouse of a member-is someone on whom this House has no right to lay a law or a rule. It is bad enough that they made the fatal error of getting involved with a politician. It is worse yet that they should have to make public every sense of their business dealings. That is wrong. I believe it is wrong. There are some who advocate that they ought to, but I fail to see that. If you leave it up to the member to make the declaration where he or she has knowledge of a conflict or where one might exist, I think those of us who are elected deserve to bear the heat. That is as far as I am prepared to go.
If I know that my spouse has a conflict of interest in some way, the fact that she is married to me makes it a conflict. The woman deserves sainthood in the first place but in the second instance, she does not deserve to be punished again. If there is a conflict, it is my obligation as an elected member to point it out. I think that covers as much as needs to be covered there, but disclosure is important.
The most important thing-this is difficult, and we are going to argue about this a lot-is a clear, straightforward process for resolving conflict. It is not easy to do. It will not be done by burying it under tonnes of paper. It is not done by setting up a huge bureaucracy. It is not accomplished by trying to bamboozle the public.
The jurisdictions where I saw it working well had this as a hallmark, a simple straightforward system with not very many people involved. It had one clear set of rules being given out, one set of advice being given, one person telling the members what they can and cannot do.
March 29, 1993

It is as simple and as straightforward as that. It must be able to deal with problems efficiently.
We have a criminal court system which is elaborate to deal with criminal charges and that is fair. I agree with that. What we are talking about is something quite different.
I know that in many places they use some version of what is called in the committee report a jurisconsult. This bill calls for a commission as well. Let me give my version of that.
This is not a person who has to be all-wise or all-knowing. It is a person who must have a reasonable amount of common sense and an understanding of what the public expects from people who are elected. In other words, it must be a person who knows what is right, what is wrong and what is reasonable. That is the hallmark of the job, not an elaborate staff, not a complicated process. In fact, in my experience, it is a fairly straightforward process.
That brings me to the first major problem I have with this bill. I do not want to vote against it because this process may work but I frankly will be surprised if it does. It seems to me it sets up two levels of advice, two sets of rules, a commission on one side and a jurisconsult on the other. I always find it dangerous in politics to set out dual tracks.
This may work. It may be possible that the Government of Canada will do something that no other government in the world has ever been able to do; create two bureaucracies that do not at some point collide like mad.
I think they will. In addition to what is written in this bill there will, of course, be regulations. There will be interpretations of regulations. There will be rules. There will be interpretations of rules. There will be advice to the members. There will be memos written to the members. There will be rulings given. If the rulings are not the same for everybody, this bill is in trouble. That is the first thing where I think this bill may be in trouble. It may not work.
I am willing to give it a shot. I understand, as everybody does, that there is a big difference between a little guy like the member from Oshawa sitting over here, just about Perth, Ontario, in the Chamber and the big wheels who sit right at the front and make all the big
Government Orders
decisions in cabinet. Behind the big wheels are the little wheels, the parliamentary secretaries.
I do not give out government contracts. I do not decide national policy. I do not decide who gets all the jobs. The opportunities for me to have a conflict are pretty rare. People in the cabinet face an entirely different set of circumstances. Sometimes parliamentary secretaries do. Sometimes they have even less influence over things than I do. But every jurisdiction that I know of which has looked at conflict of interest legislation recognizes that there are some of the players who are going to be in conflict positions much more often than others.
This bill tries to do it by dual tracks. I think the dual tracks are going to collide at some point and will cause a major problem.
To conclude fairly quickly, a couple of things do need to be said. Mr. Justice Parker in a very elaborate report gave us his opinion on the matter. One of my constituents, Michael Starr, and one of his colleagues in the Parliament of Canada, Mitchell Sharp, had their version of what should be done. The joint committee had its version of what should be done. The government has now brought forward a bill.
No matter what might happen, it is better to have an imperfect law than no law. I offer my support, tentative though it might be in spots, because I believe very strongly that whatever the rules are, as long as you write them down, we will all live with them and we will work our way through them.
It is going to be critical that we go through these things on a regular basis. If somebody gets off the hook because a definition put in this bill does not quite cover the act he is alleged to have committed, then the whole thing is a failure. That is one of the reasons why I advocated in committee, as did others, that there be no tight little definition of a conflict of interest, that it should be as broad as possible.
Those of us who worked on the joint committee have an obligation to say our little piece. Nobody wants to delay this process. I hope it is the government's intention to proceed with this legislation and to make it law now. If it has flaws we will try to pick them up as it goes through committee.

March 29, 1993
Adjournment Debate
I hope the government will listen to members with other points of view and see if it can do what I thought the joint committee did an excellent job of doing; not trying to find everyone's theory of it all, but something that is practical and will work and will assist us all in restoring a little bit of confidence. I concur with what some others members have said. I am not a great believer in a magic bill that can be passed which will make the world change its view about this place. However, there are things that members here can do, and this bill is one of them.

Mr. Speaker, this question arises out of the recently announced policy of the government to replace face to face interviews for immigration applications by the mailing in of complex forms to centrally located offices and in particular, to a new centralized office in Vegreville, Alberta which will open in April 1994.
This government proposal has already led to the closing of many local immigration offices which were accessible to people all over the country. They will be replaced as I say by fewer employees in fewer far away offices, in particular in Vegreville.
Faced with that new policy, on February 24 I asked the minister why the government was proceeding with this plan when the pilot projects were a failure and when they showed that this system would be extremely inefficient and would open the door to criminality.
I am informed by some of the people who took part in some of these pilot projects that what used to take three to four days in face to face interviews, getting the appointment or sitting before an immigration officer and going over the immigration application now takes three to four weeks in the pilot projects.
One of the major problems is that many of these people do not speak English or French as their mother tongue. In filling out these forms they make mistakes. The forms are sent back. They are returned again to the centralized office always by mail. Veiy often it takes a long time to settle the problem and get the application form dealt with. These are application forms for work visas, visitors' visas, family class applications and so on.
While it makes it more difficult for legitimate refugees in this new mail-in centralized system, it makes it easier for the criminal element because it is easier for the criminal element to defraud the documents. They do not
March 29, 1993

have to face an immigration officer across the table and it is easier to get through contrived and falsified documents in order to have illegal immigrants enter this country.
What is going to happen as a result of this policy is that more and more of a burden is going to be shifted to the offices of members of Parliament, to agencies, to NGOs and to churches. They will have to help immigrants fill out these complex forms and send them into the offices. In many cases the immigrants will probably turn to lawyers and immigration consultants which will cost them a lot of money.
I ask once again for the government either to cancel this project which is inefficient and leads to criminality or at the very least to postpone it for one year while we have a parliamentary committee look at it objectively and see if it really is in the best interests of the country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 5.37 p.m.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government announced a series of initiatives for the reconfiguration of the points of service network for the future delivery of the immigration program. These initiatives are totally consistent with the fiscal constraints announced by the President of the Treasury Board on December 2, 1992.
With fiscal restraint messages recently being announced by all levels and political stripes of government, Canadians understand there is a growing need to manage more wisely our limited tax dollars.
The restructured Canadian Immigration Centre network will provide effective client service in an efficient manner while saving the taxpayers money. The advanced use of technology in the case processing centre scheduled to begin operations in April 1994 and the efficient mail-in forms are the key to saving $6.5 million.
Some of the resource savings realized will be allocated to enhance the enforcement aspects of the immigration program thereby strengthening its integrity, something for which many Canadians have long been calling.
Even though it saves taxpayers money, our strategy maintains client service at a high level. Of the existing 64 points of service we will maintain a community presence
Adjournment Debate
with full-time immigration staff in 51 locales. This is not a rampant reduction of the inland delivery network but a refined structure that maintains a presence in small communities where appropriate, while placing the bulk of our resources in larger communities where there is a high demand for service.
In conclusion, after two years of processing case work by mail in Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver surveys confirm a client satisfaction rate of 84 per cent. Our monitoring has shown no increase in attempted misrepresentation or document fraud over personal service.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in December of last year I questioned the minister of employment regarding changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
In particular, I asked him to set out clear guidelines for proving just cause as it relates to sexual harassment. The government it is true has broadened the definition of just cause and has given the board of referees clearer powers to protect the privacy of victims. While this is fine these measures do not change the procedure for proving just cause and in consequence not much has changed for women victims.
Sexual harassment has been grounds for just cause for quite some time but the process of proof is where the failure of the system lies. As I said in December I spent four years as chair of the unemployment insurance appeal board in Halifax. I know what it takes to prove just cause. It is a long and tortuous and potentially costly endeavour and frequently it is very degrading for the female victims.
The system works against voluntary quitters and not for them. All it takes is a telephone call to the employer who will obviously deny that he sexually harassed his employee and that is it. A woman may appeal the decision to the Board of Referees but Employment and Immigrations figures show that the board only overturns the decisions of the UI officer who made the original decision 0.4 per cent of the time.
I am happy to say that when I was chair of that appeal board my ratio of overturning decisions was 25 per cent but gone are those days.

March 29, 1993
Adjournment Debate
To add insult to injury the employer is not even compelled to go before the board. He cannot be compelled to go before the board. His appearance at a separate hearing is by invitation which he is of course free to decline.
Under the old rules the complainant could still receive a portion of her UI claim. Under the new rules that this government so typically rammed through this House this will no longer be the case and women victims will lose their UI right off the top.
May I remind this House and the minister in particular that I am not as he said: "spreading lies" by stating unequivocally that women will not be protected under the new legislation any more than they were protected under the old. I suppose that if a woman has the strength, the courage and the money she can hire a lawyer and go through the process of appeal to a judge of the federal court. However, we are talking about women in this particular category most of whom make $20,000 a year or less. They are hardly the kind of clients who can afford to hire a lawyer for this kind of case.
May I remind the minister of another given that women are poorer than men. Women earn on average 30 cents less than men according to the most recent Statistics Canada report on the earnings of men and women. Do I need to again state the obvious? The wage difference between men and women will all but preclude further action by women if their UI claim is rejected.
Mr. Speaker, this piece of legislation is a disgrace.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 5.37 p.m.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows it was this government that first incorporated sexual harassment in the UI Act as just cause for leaving a job. This was done as part of the changes to the UI Act through Bill C-21.
I might add that the hon. member was one of many Liberal members who on October 25, 1990 voted against the government amendment which enshrined sexual harassment in the UI Act as just cause for quitting a job.
The hon. member also knows that CEC employees have a long history and an excellent record of dealing fairly and sensitively with all UI claimants including
those who may have quit their jobs due to sexual harassment.
We will be building on this record of fairness by providing awareness training to reinforce the sensitivity of EIC staff to the issue by issuing guidelines that will ensure that staff continue to give the benefit of the doubt to the claimant and by adopting administrative policies that allow sexual harassment cases to be handled by UI agents of the same gender and by having appeals held in private.
Bill C-113 is about fairness. It is not fair that Canadians should pay UI for people who choose not to work for no good reason. However, if just cause such as sexual harassment does exist one can be sure that the claimant will receive UI benefits. Bill C-113 is also about responsibility. It is irresponsible to continue allowing the UI deficit to increase and we must act on this.
Bill C-113 is about fairness and responsibility and I urge the hon. member to support this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier in this House I raised a question with the Minister of Public Works with regard to what I can only call either Tory mathematics or now the missing $7 million.
The matter arose because of the dispute over the proposal to build the fixed link to Prince Edward Island. As members of this House will know, P.E.I. is currently serviced by Marine Atlantic. As the courts have confirmed, as part of a constitutional requirement ferry service must be provided.
The current funding of Marine Atlantic provides for some revenue from the fare box, in other words the people who use the ferry, and another element around $23 million, $24 million or $25 million a year which comes as a subsidy from the taxpayers of Canada. That is the shortfall between the cost of the service and the fare box.
I rose in this House and raised with the Minister of Public Works the question that if it was only costing the taxpayer $23.5 million to $24 million a year to subsidize the ferry operation, why was the Government of Canada
March 29, 1993

prepared to provide up to $42 million a year to subsidize the owner and operator of a bridge.
The minister responded in the House. When Bill C-110 went to committee, I pursued the matter there with the minister. He gave me sort of a general response and then left it to the officials from Transport Canada to respond in more detail. This is where it really gets interesting. The Director General of Marine Policy and Programs, Mr. Andre Pageot, responded to my questions. Basically what he said was that the $7.7 million was a figure that they made up.
That is not money that goes to Marine Atlantic that it can put away for a day in which it needs to re-equip the fleet or replace a particular ferry. No, the Government of Canada does not put it in a special interest-bearing account so that when Marine Atlantic needs a capital infusion of the $50 million to $60 million that a new vessel would cost the money would be there. No, it does not exist there either. However, it is there to use as a basis for justifying a $42 million subsidy to the owners and operators of a bridge.
The reason that we raised objections to the fixed link is not just because of the environment, although that is a very, very important element. As we saw, the Federal Court agreed with members of the New Democratic Party and with Friends of the Island and ordered a new and proper environmental assessment.
We saw in the House earlier today the Minister of the Environment skating around the issue and not coming out and saying: "Of course we will ensure that there is a full and proper environmental assessment". He sidestepped the issue, just as the Minister for Public Works refuses to recognize the reality that this bridge project is going to cost the taxpayers more than the current ferry service does today or will in the future.
That is what this government has to be held accountable for and that is why we will continue to oppose this foolish waste of taxpayers' money.

Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan, we want to say that much has been made of the annual subsidy that would be paid to the developer of the bridge between Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. He should know that the subsidy represents the avoidable
Adjournment Debate
future costs to the federal government of maintaining the Borden ferry service that is projected over the next 35 years.
The amount of money available, as he mentioned, is $42 million calculated in 1992 dollars. This $42 million includes not only the estimated costs of operating and maintaining these ferries, but also the capital costs that would eventually be required to replace these very expensive vessels, a cost, as the hon. member would know, that is escalating year by year.
The member should know that the replacement cost is not assumed by Marine Atlantic and is not included in its subsidy.
Nevertheless it is a very real cost to the federal government, no matter which pocket it comes from. It was and is a future expense that must be taken into account when considering the value of the subsidy for the fixed link.
I thank the hon. member for raising the question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 1, 19921 raised once again on the floor of the House of Commons concerns that I have had with regard to the Westray coal mine disaster that took place in Nova Scotia.
At that time I repeatedly asked the Prime Minister and ministers of the Crown if they would conduct a federal inquiry. The answer was in the negative, the rationale being that the Government of Nova Scotia was going to proceed with an inquiry.
The fact of the matter is that what I had asked for was a federal inquiry with regard to the role of the Government of Canada and in particular the funding that the government gave to that particular operation.
We now know today, as a result of information made public, that the Government of Nova Scotia has lost $12 million, the Government of Canada has lost in excess of $80 million and 26 miners have lost their lives. As I speak in this Chamber their families are without information, which is presently in the hands of the government, as to what has happened and what is likely to happen with regard to possible criminal charges.

March 29, 1993
Adjournment Debate
This is a tragedy of national and international importance. What we found out today is that the government, under the auspices of the Freedom of Information Act, has made available to me a document from 1990 entitled The Funding of the Westray Coal Mine. It is 18 pages in length, but it is censored.
I remind this Chamber that a former President of the United States had an 18-minute gap on his tapes. What we have here is an 18-page gap with regard to the Westray coal mine. It is high time that the parliamentary secretary opposite and all members of the cabinet come clean with the people of Pictou county as to what is contained in that particular memorandum.
There was a CANMET study which was referred to in this House by ministers of the Crown, which the opposition was led to believe was the conclusive information concerning CANMET. We found out today that there are seven additional pages that have been censored by the Government of Canada. Twenty-five pages of important information have now been hidden by the government.
I want to ask the parliamentary secretary to make this information available to shed light on a tragedy in Canadian mining history. He should not stand in his place and give us that holus-bolus argument that somehow it has to be protected because of privacy. Twenty-six men have lost their lives, $12 million has gone down the tubes in Nova Scotia, and $80 million has gone down the tubes federally. Canadians have a right to know. Who is this government trying to protect, and why is it hiding this information from taxpayers in this country and from families who have been distressed over the last 12 months?
On behalf of those families I ask the parliamentary secretary opposite to provide that information so that Canadians will know exactly what happened.
Mr. Ken James (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs) Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond who I know has a very deep and concerned interest in this subject.
What I am going to say to him in some cases I think he probably already knows. For the record, under the Constitution the regulation of the mines is a provincial
responsibility. The responsibility pertains to all aspects of mine plan approval, amendment and ongoing monitoring, including health and safety. The only exceptions are Devco, which is a Crown corporation, and uranium mines.
Following the accident at the Westray coal mine in Pictou county the Government of Nova Scotia established under its jurisdiction a commission of inquiry with a mandate to determine the cause of the explosion and to examine events leading up to the accident. The federal government co-operated with the commission up until the time it was found to be invalid on constitutional grounds. That decision was successfully appealed by both the miners' union and the Nova Scotia provincial government.
In January the status of the inquiry was confirmed as valid by the appeals division of the Nova Scotia Supreme Court, although public hearings were delayed until the provincial charges and the criminal investigation were complete.
Originally, as the hon. member would know, 52 charges were laid by the province under the Occupational Health and Safety Act. In December, 34 of those charges were stayed in order to avoid jeopardizing any criminal charges.
Recently, on March 4, the remaining 18 provincial charges were stayed for similar reasons. Once the criminal investigation by the RCMP is complete and any subsequent charges have been dealt with the commission is free to resume hearings into the cause of the accident.
For its part, the federal government will continue to co-operate with the commission of inquiry established by the province of Nova Scotia to examine events leading up to the accident at the Westray coal mine.
To do more than this is not possible without infringing on the jurisdiction of the province.
